title: Living light: how a glow is made, how it is read, and why eyes need the dark

summary.text: Switch off every light and at first you see nothing. After about twenty minutes you can see the room again, though no lamp has been lit. Your eyes have changed. A firefly's flash is made by chemistry that needs four ingredients, and your eye catches that flash with chemistry too. In this unit your child tests how much more their eyes can see after waiting in the dark, finds out why heat stops a helper chemical from working, and plays a game in which a group of fireflies flashes together with no leader.
summary.art: A child sitting in a dark room beside a glow stick under a stack of paper sheets, with a faint blue glow showing through the top sheets and a few tiny fireflies in the window.

intro.hook: Walk out of bright sunshine into a dark cupboard. For a minute you see nothing at all. Stay there, and shapes begin to appear. Nothing in the cupboard has changed. What has?
intro.text: Your eyes have been changing, step by step, so that they can catch very faint light. A firefly's flash is faint light too, made by chemistry inside their body. In this unit you find out what a flash needs, why a helper chemical stops working in hot water, and how a squid and a crowd of bacteria make one lamp together. You also test how much your own eyes can see in the dark, and play a game in which fireflies with different beats learn to flash as one.
intro.art: A child stepping from a sunny doorway into a dark room, with a firefly glowing faintly at the far end of the room.

outcomes: I can name the four things a firefly's flash needs, luciferin, luciferase, oxygen and ATP, and say what each one does.
I can explain what an enzyme is, and show with a potato that heat can stop a helper chemical working.
I can tell apart a glow that is made by chemistry, a glow that is sent back at once (fluorescence) and a glow that is stored (phosphorescence).
I can explain why most deep-sea animals make blue light, and why blue light is the kind that travels furthest in sea water.
I can run a fair test to show how my eyes change in the dark, and explain it with rod cells and rhodopsin.
I can explain how glowing bacteria count each other, and how a squid and bacteria make one lamp together.
I can explain how a crowd of fireflies can flash together with no leader.
I can say what scientists agree on, what they still argue about, and how scientists use living light as a tool.

terms.meaning: Light made by a living being, using a chemical reaction inside their body. Say it like this: bye-oh-loo-mi-NESS-ence.
terms.example: A firefly's flash and the blue sparkle of a breaking wave at night are both bioluminescence.
terms.art: A firefly with a glowing lantern at the end of their body, on a dark leaf.

terms.meaning: The chemical that gives out light when it reacts with oxygen. The name comes from a Latin word meaning light-bringer.
terms.example: A firefly's luciferin is stored in the cells of their lantern, ready to use.
terms.art: A small glowing molecule drawn as a few coloured balls inside a lantern cell.

terms.meaning: The helper chemical, an enzyme, that makes luciferin react quickly.
terms.example: Without luciferase, luciferin and oxygen would react far too slowly to give a flash.
terms.art: A large curled molecule gripping a small luciferin molecule, like a hand holding a seed.

terms.meaning: A helper chemical, made by a living being, that makes one particular reaction go much faster. The enzyme is not used up, so it can do the job again and again.
terms.example: Raw potato holds an enzyme that breaks hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, so it fizzes.
terms.art: A big curled enzyme with a groove, a small molecule fitting into the groove, and two smaller pieces leaving.

terms.meaning: A small chemical that every living cell uses to carry energy to the places where energy is needed. The letters stand for adenosine triphosphate.
terms.example: Your muscles, a growing plant and a firefly's lantern all spend ATP.
terms.art: A cell drawn as a small room with tiny coins labelled ATP being carried from a power station to a lantern.

terms.meaning: Light made by a chemical reaction, whether or not anything alive is involved. Living light is chemiluminescence inside a living being.
terms.example: A glow stick and a firefly both make chemiluminescence, but only the firefly's is also living light.
terms.art: A glow stick and a firefly side by side, joined by a bracket labelled light from a chemical reaction.

terms.meaning: Light that a thing sends out at the same moment it takes in light of another colour, usually a colour we cannot see. It stops as soon as the light shining on it stops.
terms.example: A yellow highlighter line glows brightly under a UV torch, and goes dark the moment the torch is switched off.
terms.art: A highlighter line on paper glowing bright yellow-green under a purple torch beam.

terms.meaning: Light that a thing stores and gives back slowly, so it goes on glowing after the light shining on it has gone.
terms.example: A glow-in-the-dark star keeps glowing for many minutes after you switch the lamp off.
terms.art: A glow-in-the-dark star on a dark ceiling with a faint green halo.

terms.meaning: Light with more energy than violet, which our eyes cannot see. It is a part of sunlight. Too much of it can harm skin and eyes.
terms.example: A shopkeeper's UV torch makes parts of banknotes glow.
terms.art: A strip showing the colours of light from red to violet, with a hatched zone beyond violet labelled ultraviolet.

terms.meaning: The distance from the top of one light wave to the top of the next. Red light has a long wavelength. Blue light has a shorter one.
terms.example: Blue light has a shorter wavelength than red light, and each tiny packet of blue light carries more energy.
terms.art: Two wavy lines, a long slow red wave and a short quick blue wave, with the distance between peaks marked.

terms.meaning: The thin layer at the back of the eye that catches light and turns it into signals for the brain.
terms.example: The retina is like the screen at the back of a pinhole camera, but it is made of living cells.
terms.art: A side view of an eye with the retina drawn as a curved layer at the back and light coming in through the pupil.

terms.meaning: A light-catching cell in the retina that works in very dim light but cannot tell colours. Each eye has about a hundred million of them.
terms.example: At night, rod cells let you see the shape of a tree, but not what colour the leaves are.
terms.art: A thin rod-shaped cell in the retina with a small flash of light hitting its tip.

terms.meaning: A light-catching cell in the retina that needs bright light but can tell colours. Each eye has a few million of them.
terms.example: In daylight, cone cells let you tell a red chilli from a green one.
terms.art: A cone-shaped cell in the retina in three colours: red, green and blue.

terms.meaning: The light-catching chemical inside rod cells. When one packet of light hits it, it changes shape and starts a signal. It must then be built back before it can work again.
terms.example: Bright light uses up a lot of rhodopsin. That is why you see so little when you first enter a dark room.
terms.art: A purple molecule with a bent part snapping straight when a tiny light packet hits it.

terms.meaning: The slow change by which your eyes become able to see in dim light. It takes about twenty to thirty minutes to finish.
terms.example: After twenty minutes in a dark room, you can see a glow that was invisible at the start.
terms.art: Four pictures of the same dark room, the first almost black, the last showing a table, a door and a window.

terms.meaning: The way bacteria count their own crowd. Each one gives off a signal chemical, and when enough has built up they all change what they do together. Say it like this: KWOR-um.
terms.example: Glowing bacteria stay dark when few of them are together, and all switch on their light when many are.
terms.art: A few bacteria with a thin cloud of signal dots drifting away, and a crowded group with a thick cloud around them and all glowing.

terms.meaning: Two different kinds of living beings that live closely together, each getting something from the other.
terms.example: A squid gives glowing bacteria a home and food, and the bacteria give the squid a lamp.
terms.art: A small squid with a glowing patch on the underside, and tiny bacteria drawn inside the patch.

terms.meaning: A body part made to make or hold light. It may have a lens, a shutter and a mirror, like a tiny torch.
terms.example: A flashlight fish has a light organ under each eye that they can cover with a flap of skin.
terms.art: A small fish with a glowing oval under the eye and a flap of skin half covering it.

terms.meaning: Many things doing the same thing at the same moment. Fireflies in synchrony flash together. Say it like this: SIN-kruh-nee.
terms.example: In some mangrove trees, thousands of fireflies blink on and off in step.
terms.art: A tree at night covered in fireflies, half the tree dark and half lit, in the same moment.

terms.meaning: A protein from a glowing jellyfish that glows green under blue light. Scientists attach it to other proteins to see where they are inside a living cell.
terms.example: A scientist adds the gene for GFP to a nerve cell, and the whole nerve cell lights up green under a microscope.
terms.art: A microscope picture of a branching nerve cell glowing green on a dark background.

terms.meaning: How much of the energy put into something comes out as what we wanted. The rest is wasted, usually as heat.
terms.example: An old bulb with a thin wire gives out only a small part of its energy as light and the rest as heat, so it has low efficiency.
terms.art: A bulb with a big red arrow of heat and a small yellow arrow of light coming out of it.

explanations.concept: Four ways a thing can shine: hot, made, sent back at once, or stored
explanations.context: In the first Living light unit you learned that a firefly makes their own light. This card sorts all the ways a thing can give out light, so you can tell them apart.
explanations.definition: A thing can shine because it is hot, because a chemical reaction makes light, because it sends light back at once in another colour (fluorescence), or because it stores light and lets it out slowly (phosphorescence).
explanations.description: A candle flame and an old bulb shine because they are very hot. A firefly and a glow stick shine because a chemical reaction makes light, with almost no heat. Fluorescence is different again. Under a UV torch, a highlighter line takes in ultraviolet light that your eyes cannot see, and sends out visible light at the same moment. When the torch goes off, the glow goes off with it. Phosphorescence is a stored glow. A glow-in-the-dark star keeps some of the light that fell on it and lets it out for minutes or hours. A simple test tells them apart. Switch off the light that was shining on the thing. If the glow stops at once, it was fluorescence. If it fades slowly, it was stored. If it carries on in total darkness with nothing shining on it, the thing is making its own light. The Moon is none of these. The Moon only bounces sunlight back.
examples: A firefly's flash carries on in a pitch dark field, so it is made by chemistry.
A highlighter line stops glowing the moment the UV torch is switched off, so it is fluorescence.
A glow-in-the-dark star fades slowly over many minutes, so it is stored light.
explanations.art: Four small panels: a candle flame, a firefly, a highlighter under a purple torch and a glow-in-the-dark star, each labelled with how it shines.

explanations.concept: A firefly's flash needs four ingredients
explanations.context: You know that a firefly mixes luciferin with oxygen to make light. This card adds two more ingredients that scientists found later, and explains why every flash costs the firefly energy.
explanations.definition: A firefly's flash needs luciferin, the helper chemical luciferase, oxygen, and ATP, the small chemical cells use to carry energy.
explanations.description: Luciferin is the chemical that gives out the light. Luciferase is the enzyme that makes the reaction quick. Oxygen arrives through tiny air tubes. ATP is the fourth ingredient, and it is the one that is easy to miss. ATP is a small packet of energy that every living cell makes and spends. Your muscles spend it, and so does every plant. In a firefly's lantern, ATP first gets the luciferin ready, and then oxygen turns it into light. So every flash costs the firefly some of the energy from their food. In 1947, the American scientist William McElroy found that a firefly lantern extract, mixed in a test tube, glowed only when ATP was added. Without ATP the glow died away. When he added a new drop of ATP, the glow came back.
examples: A flash costs the firefly ATP, in the same way a step costs your muscles ATP.
A firefly lantern extract in a tube glows for a short while and fades, and glows again when ATP is added.
The more ATP there is, the brighter a mixture of firefly luciferin and luciferase glows.
explanations.art: A lantern drawn as a small room: ATP coins, luciferin, luciferase and oxygen all going in, and a flash of light coming out.

explanations.concept: Enzymes: helpers that speed up one job and are not used up
explanations.context: Luciferase is called a helper chemical. This card says what kind of helper it is, because your own body is full of the same kind of helpers.
explanations.definition: An enzyme is a protein made by a living being that makes one particular reaction go much faster. The enzyme itself is not used up.
explanations.description: A reaction that would take days or years can take a fraction of a second when the right enzyme is there. An enzyme has a groove of exactly the right shape. The small molecules fit into the groove, are pushed together, and come out changed. Then the enzyme is free to do the job again. A single enzyme can do this thousands of times in a second. Because an enzyme works by its shape, anything that bends the shape stops the enzyme. Heat does this. If you boil an enzyme, it loses its shape and cannot grip anything. That is why cooking changes raw food, and why a boiled potato will not fizz in hydrogen peroxide. Very cold temperatures do not bend the shape. They only slow the enzyme down. Your cells use thousands of different enzymes. Luciferase is one that happens to make light.
examples: Catalase in raw potato breaks hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen gas, so the potato fizzes.
Enzymes in your spit start to break down starch in a roti as you chew it.
Boiling milk stops many of its enzymes, because heat bends them out of shape.
explanations.art: A large enzyme with a groove, a molecule fitting in, two pieces leaving, and then a boiled enzyme with a bent groove that nothing fits into.

explanations.concept: Cold light: how much of the energy comes out as light
explanations.context: In the first Living light unit you found out that a glow stick feels cold. This card puts a number on how well different lights turn energy into light.
explanations.definition: A light is efficient if most of the energy it uses comes out as light. Living light is far more efficient than an old bulb, but it is not perfect.
explanations.description: An old bulb with a thin wire inside turns only about 5 parts in every 100 of its electrical energy into light. The other 95 parts become heat. That is why such a bulb is too hot to touch. Modern LED bulbs do much better and stay cooler. A firefly's reaction does even better, but only at one step: the moment the light is made. In a lab in 2008, scientists reported that about 4 in every 10 firefly luciferin molecules that reacted gave out a flash of light. But that is one step in a chain. The firefly still spends energy to make luciferin, to carry oxygen and to make ATP. So living light wastes very little at the moment the light is made, but the whole animal still spends food to shine. No living being gets light for nothing.
examples: An old filament bulb gives out about 5 parts of light for every 95 parts of heat.
About 4 in every 10 firefly luciferin molecules that react are reported to give out light. Very little is wasted as heat, which is why a firefly's flash feels cool.
A glow stick's light does not need a battery, but the glow ends when the chemicals run out.
explanations.art: Two bars side by side: an old bulb with a tall heat part and a tiny light part, and a firefly with a bigger light part and a smaller heat part.

explanations.concept: Why most deep-sea light is blue
explanations.context: Deep-sea animals use light to catch food, hide, scare and talk. This card asks why so many of them use the same colour.
explanations.definition: Sea water takes in red light very quickly and lets blue light travel furthest, so most deep-sea animals make blue light and have eyes that see blue best.
explanations.description: Sunlight is a mix of all the colours. As it goes down into the sea, the water takes in each colour at a different speed. Red is nearly gone within about ten metres. Orange and yellow go next. Green goes deeper. Blue goes furthest. So below a few hundred metres, the only light left from the Sun is a faint blue. Blue light also travels furthest through the water, so a blue light can be seen from far away. That is why many deep-sea animals make blue light, and why their eyes are best at catching blue. The colour of the light depends on the shape of the luciferase, the enzyme that helps make it. A small change in the luciferase's shape can change the colour. There are exceptions. Some deep-sea fish, such as certain dragonfish, make red light that most animals around them cannot see, which is like having a secret torch.
examples: A red cloth looks black at 20 metres under the sea, because the red light has already been taken in by the water above.
A hatchetfish's belly lights are blue, to match the faint blue light that comes down from above.
A firefly on land makes yellow-green light, because the night air does not take in colours as sea water does.
explanations.art: A cross-section of the sea, with coloured light fading from red at the top to deep blue at the bottom and a blue-glowing fish at the bottom.

explanations.concept: How your eyes see in dim light
explanations.context: A firefly's flash is faint. This card explains how your eye catches faint light, and why it needs time to do it well.
explanations.definition: Your retina has two kinds of light catchers. Rod cells work in dim light and see no colour. Cone cells work in bright light and see colour.
explanations.description: Each eye has about a hundred million rod cells and a few million cone cells. In a bright room, the cones do most of the seeing. In a dark room the cones can no longer catch enough light, and the rods must take over. Rod cells hold a light-catching chemical called rhodopsin. One packet of light, called a photon, can change one rhodopsin molecule, and a rod cell can respond to even one photon. But bright light uses up rhodopsin. After bright light, the rods have little left, so you see almost nothing. In the dark your cells build rhodopsin back, a little at a time. This takes about twenty to thirty minutes. Your pupils also open wider within seconds, but the chemical change matters more. This is also why a red torch is kinder to eyes that have got used to the dark. Rods are much less sensitive to red, so red light uses up much less rhodopsin.
examples: A person who steps out of a bright street into a dark cinema cannot see the seats for a minute or two.
A pilot or sailor uses a dim red lamp at night so that their eyes stay used to the dark.
Faint stars seem to disappear when you look straight at them, because the middle of your retina has few rod cells.
explanations.art: A cross-section of a retina with tall rod cells and short cone cells, and a ray of light reaching a rod.

explanations.concept: Seeing is chemistry too: a firefly's glow in reverse
explanations.context: A firefly turns chemical energy into light. This card shows that your eye does the same job the other way round.
explanations.definition: In a rod cell, a packet of light changes the shape of a rhodopsin molecule, and that starts a chain of chemical steps that ends in a signal to the brain.
explanations.description: In a firefly, a chemical reaction ends with a packet of light being given out. In your eye, a packet of light starts a chemical reaction. When light hits rhodopsin, a part of the molecule snaps from a bent shape to a straight one. That change sets off a chain of reactions inside the rod cell, and the cell sends an electrical signal along the optic nerve. So the chain goes from the firefly's food, to their ATP, to their flash, to the rhodopsin in your eye, to the signal in your nerve, to what you see. Light is the bridge between two chemical events, one in the sender and one in the receiver. The rhodopsin must be built back afterwards, which is why your eyes take minutes to get ready for the dark.
examples: A firefly turns chemical energy into a flash. Your rod cell turns the flash back into a chemical change.
A camera turns light into numbers. An eye turns light into chemical change, then into nerve signals.
Plants also catch light with chemistry, using chlorophyll, and turn it into food.
explanations.art: A firefly on the left, a flash of light across the middle, and an eye on the right, with chemistry labelled at both ends.

explanations.concept: Bacteria that count: how quorum sensing works
explanations.context: In the first Living light unit you read that bacteria glow only when there are lots of them. This card explains how they can tell how many they are.
explanations.definition: Bacteria count their crowd by giving out a signal chemical. When the signal builds up past a level, all the bacteria change what they do at the same time.
explanations.description: A single bacterium is far too small to make a visible light. A bacterium that glowed alone in the open sea would waste energy. So each one makes a small amount of a signal chemical, and the chemical drifts away. In a big open sea, the signal spreads out and stays weak. In a small, crowded space, such as a squid's light organ, the signal builds up. When it passes a level, it switches on the genes for making light in every bacterium together. In the 1970s, the American scientists Kenneth Nealson and Woodland Hastings found that glowing bacteria stay dark until many of them are together. Later, the scientist Bonnie Bassler and her team found a second signal that many different kinds of bacteria use, like a shared language.
examples: A bacterium alone in the open sea stays dark, because their signal drifts away.
Thousands of the same bacteria packed into a squid's light organ all switch on together.
Some bacteria that cause disease also wait for a crowd before they attack, which is why scientists study how to block the signal.
explanations.art: On the left, a few bacteria with a thin cloud of signal dots drifting away in the sea. On the right, a crowd with a thick cloud and all glowing.

explanations.concept: Two beings, one lamp: the squid and the bacteria
explanations.context: This card follows the glowing bacteria into a real animal, a small squid that lives in the sea near Hawaii.
explanations.definition: The Hawaiian bobtail squid keeps glowing bacteria in a light organ under their body. The squid gives the bacteria a home and food, and the bacteria give the squid a lamp.
explanations.description: A newborn bobtail squid has no bacteria. They pick them up from the sea water, and only one kind of bacteria, Vibrio fischeri, is allowed to stay. The squid hunts at night in shallow water. On a moonlit night, the squid would show from below as a dark shadow against the light from above. The light organ shines a little blue light downwards to cancel the shadow, matching the brightness of the moonlight. The organ even has a lens, a shutter and light-sensing cells, so the squid can adjust their lamp as the moon changes. Each dawn the squid pushes out most of their bacteria into the sea, and the few that are left multiply during the day, ready for the night. The scientist Margaret McFall-Ngai has studied this partnership for many years.
examples: The squid's light organ has a lens that spreads the light and a shutter that can dim it.
The squid pushes most of their bacteria out at dawn. The few that are left multiply during the day, so the crowd is ready again by night.
Your own gut is full of bacteria that live with you, and help you digest food.
explanations.art: A small squid seen from below, with a glowing patch on the underside, and an enlarged picture of the light organ with a lens and a shutter.

explanations.concept: Fireflies that flash together, with no leader
explanations.context: In the first Living light unit you read that in some trees, thousands of fireflies blink on and off as one. This card says how they might do it.
explanations.definition: In some kinds of fireflies, a crowd flashes in step because each firefly has an inner timer and adjusts it slightly when they see a neighbour's flash.
explanations.description: In 1935, an American scientist named Hugh Smith described fireflies in Thailand flashing together in trees. Many scientists did not believe him. They thought it was a trick of the eye. Careful studies in the 1960s and 1970s, by John Buck and Elisabeth Buck, showed that it was real. The idea is simple. Each firefly has a timer that counts up to the next flash. When a firefly sees a neighbour flash, their own timer is nudged forward, so their next flash comes a little sooner. Fireflies that flash late are nudged forward, and in a few cycles the whole crowd lines up. There is no leader. Computer models that use only this one rule also end up flashing together. But scientists have not worked out all the details for each kind of firefly. This is why we still call it an idea.
examples: In the mangroves of Malaysia and Thailand, thousands of fireflies of one kind flash in step along a river.
In 1665, the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens noticed that two pendulum clocks on the same wall swung in step.
The pacemaker cells of your heart keep time together with no boss cell, as these fireflies do with no leader.
explanations.art: A line of mangrove trees at night with every tree flashing at the same moment, and a small inner timer drawn inside one firefly.

explanations.concept: Where does the luciferin come from?
explanations.context: A firefly has luciferin in their lantern. This card asks a question that sounds easy but is not: where does the luciferin come from?
explanations.description: A glowing being needs a supply of luciferin. Some make it inside their own body. Others may collect it from what they eat. In the sea, many glowing animals use the same luciferin, called coelenterazine. Scientists have shown that some animals can make it themselves. For others, such as some small crustaceans, the evidence points to food. Fireflies are a special case. A kind of firefly called Photuris eats fireflies of another kind, and so gets their bitter defence chemicals. The scientist Thomas Eisner and his team showed this in the 1990s. But how fireflies make their own luciferin is still being worked out.
examples: Many sea animals use the same luciferin, coelenterazine, even though they are not close relatives.
A trickster Photuris female eats a male of another kind, and so gets his bitter defence chemicals.
An animal that glows only because of their food could lose the glow if the food changed.
explanations.art: A small crustacean eating a plankton and a faint glow starting inside their body, with an arrow labelled luciferin from food.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study glowing sea animals
perspectives.explanation: Some animals make coelenterazine themselves, and others seem to get it from their food. Both can be true for different animals.
Fireflies seem to make their luciferin in their own bodies, but the full steps are still being worked out.
Nobody has the complete map yet. Each new glowing animal tested may give a different answer.

explanations.context: In the first Living light unit you read that some glowing fungi glow brightest at night. This card says how scientists showed that the glow follows an inner clock.
explanations.definition: Some glowing living beings glow brightest at night even when they are kept in constant darkness, so their glow follows a clock inside their own body.
explanations.description: In the 1950s and 1960s, the scientists Woodland Hastings and Beatrice Sweeney studied a one-celled sea plankton called Gonyaulax. They found that the glow was brightest at night. When they kept these plankton in steady dim light day and night, the glow still rose and fell in a cycle of about a day. So the cycle did not come from the Sun. It came from a clock inside the plankton. A clock like this is called a circadian rhythm. The word means about a day. Plants, fungi, fireflies and people all have such clocks. A clock may save energy. A glowing being that expects the night can get ready before dark, and need not make light in the day when nobody could see it.
examples: Gonyaulax, a glowing sea plankton, glows more at night even when kept in constant dim light.
Some glowing fungi are brightest at night, and dim by day.
You feel sleepy at night even in a room with no windows, because of a clock in your body.
explanations.art: A graph of glow brightness rising and falling over three days in a dark box, with sun and moon icons that are crossed out.

explanations.concept: Sea sparkle, plankton blooms and the Indian seas
explanations.context: On some nights the sea near Indian beaches glows blue from sea sparkle, a tiny glowing plankton. This card is about what happens when sea sparkle multiplies into huge numbers.
explanations.description: Sea sparkle, called Noctiluca by scientists, is a one-celled plankton that glows when the water is stirred. When conditions suit them, they multiply into a bloom that can turn the sea green by day and blue by night. A form of Noctiluca that has green algae living inside them has been reported to bloom each winter in the northern Arabian Sea. Scientists including Helga do Rosario Gomes, who worked in Goa, reported in 2014 that these blooms had become much larger, and linked them to patches of low-oxygen water. Some scientists worry that blooms change the food chain, because fish may not eat Noctiluca. Others say that more years of careful records are needed before anyone can say what causes the blooms.
examples: A bloom of Noctiluca can turn the sea surface green in the day.
On a night with a bloom, every breaking wave lights up blue.
Fishers on the Indian coasts have long noticed years when the sea changes colour.
explanations.art: A coastal sea with a green-tinted bloom by day, and the same sea glowing blue at the edge of the waves at night.

perspectives.who: Scientists who studied the Arabian Sea blooms
perspectives.explanation: The blooms became larger as patches of low-oxygen water spread. Noctiluca can survive in such water better than many other plankton.
Blooms have many causes, including warm water, nutrients from land and ocean currents. More years of careful records are needed.
Everyone agrees the blooms are worth watching. What causes them and what they do to fish is still being studied.

explanations.concept: Living light as a tool: lamps for the invisible
explanations.context: Scientists have found ways to use the chemicals of living light to see things that are too small or hidden to see. This card says how.
explanations.definition: Scientists use the genes for glowing proteins as markers. If a gene is on, the cell lights up, so the light shows where the gene is working.
explanations.description: In 1962 Osamu Shimomura and his team described a green glowing protein from a jellyfish. In 1994 Martin Chalfie put the gene for it into a tiny worm, and the worm's cells glowed green. Roger Tsien later made versions in other colours. The three shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2008. Now a scientist can join the gene for the glowing protein to a gene they want to follow. Where that gene works, the cell glows. Scientists use this to watch nerve cells grow, and cancer cells spread. The firefly gives another tool. The more ATP there is, the brighter a mixture with firefly luciferase glows. So a swab wiped on a kitchen counter and tested this way glows brighter if more living cells, with more ATP, have been left there.
examples: A nerve cell with the glow gene attached to it lights up green, so a scientist can see its branches.
A hospital swab glows brighter when more living cells, and so more ATP, are on a surface.
A water sample is tested with glowing bacteria. If the glow gets dim, something in the water is poisoning them.
explanations.art: A microscope picture with one green glowing branched cell, and next to it a swab touching a counter and a small glowing tube.

explanations.concept: Bright nights: light pollution beyond fireflies
explanations.context: In the first Living light unit you saw that bright lights hide firefly flashes. This card shows that fireflies are not the only ones who need the dark.
explanations.definition: Light pollution is too much artificial light at night, and it harms many animals, not only fireflies.
explanations.description: Many animals use the dark. Baby turtles hatch at night on a beach and crawl towards the brightest, lowest horizon, which is usually the sea shining under the sky. A bright lamp on the land behind the beach can make them crawl the wrong way. On the Chennai coast, volunteer groups protect Olive Ridley turtle nests and ask nearby houses to keep lights low in the hatching season. Moths circle lamps and get tired, so they eat less and are easier to catch. Migrating birds can be pulled off course by lit towers. A bright sky also hides the stars. A dim lamp that points down gives people the light they need and leaves the dark for the animals. In 2020, firefly scientists named light pollution as one of the biggest threats to fireflies after the loss of the places where they live.
examples: Olive Ridley hatchlings can be drawn to a street lamp instead of the sea.
Moths circle a lamp for hours and have less time to feed.
In a big city you can see only a few stars, but in a village far from lights you can see hundreds.
explanations.art: A beach at night with baby turtles crawling towards the sea under a dim sky, and one lost turtle crawling towards a bright street lamp.

agreed.text: A firefly's flash needs four ingredients: luciferin, the helper luciferase, oxygen and ATP.
agreed.evidence: In 1947 William McElroy found that a firefly lantern extract glowed again when ATP was added. Labs now mix the four ingredients in a tube and make a flash on demand.

agreed.text: Enzymes work by their shape, and strong heat bends them out of shape so they stop working.
agreed.evidence: Raw potato fizzes in hydrogen peroxide and boiled potato does not. Cooking and boiling milk also stop enzymes in the same way.

agreed.text: Sea water takes in red light quickly, and blue light travels furthest, so deep sea light is blue.
agreed.evidence: Light meters lowered into the sea show red gone within about ten metres and blue left at depth. The eyes of many deep-sea animals are most sensitive to blue.

agreed.text: Eyes need about twenty to thirty minutes in the dark to see at their best.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have tested many volunteers, asking them to say when they could first see a very faint light, minute after minute in the dark. The faintest light they could see kept getting fainter for about twenty to thirty minutes.

agreed.text: Glowing bacteria light up only when many are together, because they count each other with signal chemicals.
agreed.evidence: In 1970 Kenneth Nealson and Woodland Hastings saw that glowing bacteria stay dark at low numbers and glow when the crowd is large. Later work, including Bonnie Bassler's, found the signal chemicals.

agreed.text: Some kinds of fireflies flash in step with each other.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have filmed and counted flashes in the mangroves of Southeast Asia and in forests in North America. The flashes line up closely, more than chance would explain.

agreed.text: Bright lights at night harm fireflies, and also hatchling turtles, moths and migrating birds.
agreed.evidence: In experiments, fireflies near bright lights flash less and find fewer partners. Turtle groups find that hatchlings crawl towards lamps instead of the sea.

agreed.text: The chemicals of living light make useful tools for seeing inside cells.
agreed.evidence: Green fluorescent protein from a jellyfish is used in laboratories all over the world. Shimomura, Chalfie and Tsien shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it.

challenging.claim: Fireflies that flash together must be following a leader.
challenging.who: Many people, and some scientists in the 1930s.
challenging.for: In a choir or a marching band, one person keeps the beat for everyone.
challenging.against: When Hugh Smith first described synchronous fireflies in 1935, many scientists did not believe him. Later work by John and Elisabeth Buck showed it was real. Models show a crowd can line up with each firefly only watching neighbours, and no one in charge.
challenging.context: This card looks at a common idea about groups that act together.

challenging.claim: Living light is perfectly efficient, so no energy is lost as heat.
challenging.who: A common idea about cold light.
challenging.for: A firefly's light feels cool, and lab tests found a very high share of reacting molecules give out light.
challenging.against: That share is for one step only. The firefly still spends food energy to make ATP and luciferin, and some energy leaves as heat. No living thing shines for free.
challenging.context: This card looks at an idea about cold light and energy.

challenging.claim: Your eye works like a camera, taking the same picture in light and dark.
challenging.for: An eye has a lens, a dark chamber and a layer at the back that catches light, like a camera.
challenging.against: A camera's sensor does not change its chemistry. Your retina does. Bright light uses up rhodopsin, and the dark slowly builds it back. That is why your eyes need twenty minutes.
challenging.context: This card looks at a common way of thinking about how eyes work.

challenging.claim: Heat only makes reactions go faster. It never stops them.
challenging.for: A little warmth speeds up most reactions, such as cooking dal or a glow stick shining.
challenging.against: Enzymes lose their shape in strong heat and stop working. A boiled potato has no working catalase left, so it does not fizz in hydrogen peroxide.
challenging.context: This card looks at an idea about heat and chemical reactions.

challenging.claim: The huge blooms of sea sparkle in the Arabian Sea are caused only by pollution.
challenging.for: Blooms often follow nutrients washing into the sea from land.
challenging.against: Scientists who studied the Arabian Sea also link the blooms to spreading low-oxygen water and to changes in winter winds and temperature. No single cause has been proved to explain all of it.
challenging.context: This card looks at a question about why the sea sometimes glows with huge numbers of plankton.

challenging.claim: Whenever a living being glows, the glow is a signal meant for someone to see.
challenging.for: Fireflies and many deep-sea animals use their light to talk, hide or scare.
challenging.against: Some glowing bacteria and fungi have no one to signal to. Scientists suggest the first glow may have helped with chemistry in the body, and was used as a signal only later.
challenging.context: This card looks at why living beings first began to glow.

challenging.claim: If you cannot see any light, there is no light there.
challenging.for: In a dark room, we see nothing at all.
challenging.against: A glow stick hidden behind many sheets of paper cannot be seen at first, but can be seen after twenty minutes in the dark. The light was there the whole time. The eye was not ready for it.
challenging.context: This card looks at what it means to say a place is dark.

big_questions.q: A glow stick behind ten sheets of paper is invisible at first and visible after twenty minutes. Was the light there the whole time?
big_questions.hint: Think about what changed, the light or the eye.

big_questions.q: A boiled potato does not fizz, though nothing was taken out of it. What did boiling change?
big_questions.hint: Think about the shape of an enzyme.

big_questions.q: A single bacterium cannot count. How can a crowd of bacteria know that the crowd is big enough?
big_questions.hint: Think about where a signal builds up and where it drifts away.

big_questions.q: Fireflies flash together with no leader. How could a crowd agree without anyone in charge?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each firefly does when they see a neighbour flash.

big_questions.q: Why is living light mostly blue in the deep sea, but yellow-green from a firefly in a field?
big_questions.hint: Think about which colours sea water takes in, and what the animals' eyes can see.

big_questions.q: Some deep-sea fish make red light that most animals around them cannot see. Is that cheating?
big_questions.hint: Think about whether seeing is the same for every animal.

big_questions.q: A squid and her bacteria make one lamp together. Is the lamp one being, or two?
big_questions.hint: Think about which of them could make the lamp alone.

big_questions.q: A trickster firefly copies the answer flash of another kind of firefly. How can a firefly trust a signal that could be copied?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a signal would have to cost, or what else a listener could check.

story.title: Twenty Minutes of Dark
story.note: A made-up story. Valaikuppam, Mythili, her grandmother and her uncle are imagined. The science is real. Eyes need about twenty minutes in the dark to see their best. Faint lights are easier to see out of the corner of the eye. Sea sparkle plankton really flash blue when the water around them is stirred.
text: Mythili was eleven, and she was the only person in Valaikuppam who sat in the dark on purpose.

Valaikuppam was a fishing village on the coast south of Chennai. The boats lay on the sand in long rows, like sleeping cows. Her uncle Selvam took his boat out every evening with the fleet and came back before dawn.
That week, her science teacher had said something odd. 'Your eyes need about twenty minutes in the dark to see their best,' said Revathi Miss. 'Do not believe me. Test it.'

So Mythili tested it. She sat in the bathroom with the door shut and the light off. At first she saw only a thin white line under the door. Ten minutes later she could see the shape of the bucket. After twenty minutes, she could see the tap, and the shine on the wet floor. Nothing in the bathroom had changed.
'Eyes are slow,' she told the dark.

Her grandmother laughed when she heard. 'The sea told me that before school did,' said Paati. She had cleaned fish on that beach for most of her life. 'And here is something school may not know. Never stare at a faint light, child. Look just beside it. Then it comes.'
Three weeks later, the storm came.

It was not a big storm, only a rough night with rain blown sideways. The clouds hid the Moon and the stars. At the mouth of the cove ran a long wall of black rocks, piled up to keep the waves out. There was only one gap in the wall, as wide as three boats. By day you could see it. By night, a lamp on the tallest rock showed it.
At nine o'clock, a branch fell on the wires, and the lamp on the rock went out. So did every light in the village.

The fleet was still at sea. The men on the beach shouted. They lit kerosene lamps and tied burning rags to poles. Out on the water, the captains switched on their big torches, and the beams swung across the waves.

Mythili stood at the edge of the sand and watched the torches. She noticed something. Every time a beam swept towards the shore, the whole sea turned black behind it. The men on the boats were blinding themselves.
She ran to the headman. 'Please, put out the lamps!' she said. 'Every light makes our eyes forget the dark. We must switch everything off, and wait twenty minutes with our eyes open.'

The men looked at her as if she had spoken backwards. Then Paati pushed through them, holding her sari tight against the wind. 'She is right,' said Paati. 'I have seen the sea's own lamps, in March, when the waves break. You were all here. Switch off.'

One by one, the lamps went out. Far away on the water, Selvam saw the shore go black. He remembered a girl in a bathroom. He shouted to the next boat, and the next, and one by one the torches died out at sea.

Then everyone waited. Mythili counted the minutes on her fingers, folding one down for each sixty slow counts. At five minutes, she saw the dark shapes of the boats on the sand. At ten, she saw the pale line of the shore. At fifteen, the sky had become a little lighter than the sea.
At eighteen minutes, she saw it.

Far out, where the waves struck the rocks, there was a faint blue line. When she looked straight at it, it vanished. When she looked beside it, it came back, as Paati had said. The line grew clearer. It ran along the wall to the left, and it ran along the wall to the right, and between the two lines, there was a dark gap with small blue ripples dancing in it.
'There,' she whispered. 'The gap is where it is not glowing.'

The glow came from the sea itself. Tiny living beings, each as small as a grain of sand, drifted in the water. Each one flashed blue when a wave knocked against them. Where the waves crashed on the rocks, the flashes were thickest. Where the water was calm in the gap, they were dark.

Mythili took Paati's old red-bordered cloth and wrapped it round the one torch she had kept, so that only a dim red glow showed. She held it up at the water's edge. Red light does not spoil night eyes, and out on the boats, it showed them where the beach was.
The boats came in slowly, black shapes in the black sea, steering for the dark gap between the two blue lines. Each oar left a trail of blue drops. One boat, two, five, eight. The last was Selvam's.
He jumped out into the shallow water, and the splash lit up around his knees like blue sparks. 'I saw nothing for twenty minutes,' he said, 'and then I saw everything. Who taught you that?'
'Nobody,' said Mythili. 'The light was there all the time. Our eyes just needed time to get ready for it.'

In the morning, the rocks were plain and black, and the sea was only grey. Mythili stood on the beach for a long time. She thought about the lamps she had never seen, because she had never waited long enough in the dark.
story.epiphany: A faint light can be there even when you cannot see it. Eyes need about twenty minutes in the dark to be ready to see it, and a bright lamp undoes that work in a moment.
ask: Why does shining a torch make it harder to see a faint light afterwards?
Why is it easier to see a very faint light if you look a little to one side of it?
Why is a dim red light kinder than a bright white one to eyes that have got used to the dark?
How could you tell whether a glow in water was being made by living beings, or was only sunlight bouncing off?
