flow.do: Show your child the glow stick and the stack of paper. Say that the stick will be hidden under 12 sheets. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write it down.
flow.say: This glow stick will lie under twelve sheets of paper. Each sheet hides some of the light. We will sit in a dark room and see how many sheets we can see the glow through. After twenty minutes, will we see it through more sheets, fewer sheets or the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A glow stick is hidden under 12 sheets of paper. After 20 minutes in the dark, will you see the glow through more sheets or fewer? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the number of sheets might change, or stay the same?
good: My eyes will get used to the dark.
The glow stick will get dimmer.
It will be the same, because the light does not change.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Expect to hear that the glow stick will fade. A glow stick does fade over hours, but over 20 minutes it hardly changes, and that is part of why this is a fair test of eyes.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Eyes in the Dark test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Cut six A4 sheets in half to make 12 half-sheets. Put a table and two chairs in the dark room. Block the gap under the door with a towel. Snap the glow stick and lay it flat on the table. Cover it with all 12 half-sheets, stacked neatly.
flow.say: We cut twelve half-sheets. The stick lies under all of them. Put your chair about thirty centimetres from the stack. This is where you will sit for every test.
flow.kid: Cut 6 sheets in half. Snap the glow stick. Cover it with all 12 half-sheets.
flow.parent: The room must be as dark as you can make it. A bathroom with no window works well. Mark the chair position with a small piece of tape. Check that the glow stick cannot be seen through the 12 sheets in a lit room.

check.q: Why must the stack, the stick and the seat stay in the same place for every test?
options: So only the time in the dark changes
So the stick lasts longer
So the paper stays clean
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If the stick moved closer next time, you would not know whether your eyes or the distance made the difference.

flow.context: In this step, you prepare the stack of paper and the glow stick. They stay the same for every test.

flow.do: Sit with your child in the brightest room for 3 minutes, facing a bright lamp or window. Do not look at the Sun. Then walk them, holding their hand, into the dark room.
flow.say: First we get your eyes used to bright light. Look at this bright lamp, but not too closely, for three minutes. Now come into the dark room with me. Sit in your chair, and keep your eyes open.
flow.kid: Sit in bright light for 3 minutes. Then walk into the dark room. Keep your eyes open.
flow.parent: Bright light uses up the rhodopsin in the rod cells, so the test has a clear starting point. Never let your child look at the Sun or at the bulb directly.
flow.context: In this step, you get your child's eyes used to bright light. Then you go into the dark room.

flow.do: After 1 minute in the dark, ask your child to lift the sheets off one at a time from the top. When they first see a glow, they say stop. Count the sheets left on top. Write the number. Put all the sheets back.
flow.say: You have been in the dark for one minute. Lift off the sheets one at a time. Say stop when you see the faintest glow. Now we count how many sheets are left. That is your number for one minute. Put all the sheets back.
flow.kid: Lift off sheets one by one. Say stop when you see a glow. Count the sheets left.
flow.parent: Write the number down in big digits. You can write in the dark. If your child sees the glow only after removing every sheet, write 0. If they see it through all 12 sheets, write 12 or more.

check.q: At 1 minute, your child sees the glow with only 2 sheets left on top. What does that tell you?
options: At first, their eyes could only catch a bright glow
The glow stick was brightest at the start
The glow stick was broken
check.why: Sheets hide light. Needing to take off many sheets means the glow had to be bright for the eyes to see it. Picking 'brightest at the start' misses that the stick hardly changes in 20 minutes. Picking 'broken' misses that the stick was fine and the eye was the part that changed.

flow.context: In this step, you do the first test, after one minute in the dark.

flow.do: Wait in the dark, talking quietly or telling a story. At 5 minutes, the timer rings. Your child does the sheets test again. Write the number. Put all the sheets back.
flow.say: Five minutes in the dark. Let's do the test again. Lift off the sheets one at a time. Say stop when you see the glow. How many sheets are left?
flow.kid: Wait quietly. At 5 minutes, do the sheet test again.
flow.context: In this step, you wait in the dark and do the second test, at 5 minutes.

flow.do: Keep waiting in the dark. At 10 minutes, the timer rings. Do the sheets test again. Write the number. Put all the sheets back. Do not turn on any light.
flow.say: Ten minutes. Same test again. Lift off one sheet at a time. Say stop when you see the glow. Remember, no lights, and no phone screens.
flow.kid: At 10 minutes, do the sheet test again.
flow.parent: The numbers often rise slowly at first and then more quickly. Do not tell your child what number you expect.
flow.context: In this step, you do the third test, at 10 minutes.

flow.do: Keep waiting in the dark. At 20 minutes, the timer rings. Do the sheets test again. Write the number. Then turn on the light and look at your four numbers together.
flow.say: Twenty minutes. This is the last test. Lift off one sheet at a time and say stop when you see the glow. Then we will turn the light on and look at all four numbers.
flow.kid: At 20 minutes, do the sheet test one last time. Then switch on the light.
flow.parent: If your child still sees the glow through all 12 sheets, write 12 or more, and next time use 20 sheets. If the numbers stay the same, write that down. It is still a real result. Dim glow sticks and very dark rooms give smaller numbers. Do not worry if your numbers are different from the example.

check.q: At 20 minutes, your child sees the glow with 9 sheets left. The glow stick has hardly changed. What does the change in numbers show?
options: Their eyes became able to catch fainter light
The sheets became thinner
The room became lighter
check.why: The stick, the sheets and the room were the same. The only thing that changed was the child, and so their eyes must have changed. Over about twenty minutes, the rod cells built back their rhodopsin. Picking 'the room became lighter' misses that the room had no light.

flow.context: In this step, you do the last test, at 20 minutes, and look at all four numbers together.

flow.do: Ask your child three things: what they think now, what they saw in their numbers that shows it, and why they think it happened. Draw a line graph of the four numbers, with minutes along the bottom and sheets up the side.
flow.say: Let's put it together. First, what do you think now? Second, what did you see in your numbers that shows it? Third, why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think, what you saw in your numbers, and why it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer. What I think: eyes can see fainter and fainter light the longer they are in the dark. What I saw: at 1 minute I saw the glow through a few sheets, and at 20 minutes through more. Why: the light and the stack did not change, so my eyes must have. After bright light, the rod cells need time to build back their light-catching chemical. Do not give this explanation first. Ask for the child's own idea, and then add this.
flow.think: A firefly's flash is faint. What do a watcher's eyes need before they can see it?
flow.context: In this step, you say what the numbers show, and draw a line graph.

experiments.title: The Helper That Heat Stops: raw potato, boiled potato and a bottle of peroxide
experiments.context: This is a test of an enzyme, a helper chemical. A raw potato holds an enzyme that makes hydrogen peroxide fizz. You find out what boiling does to the helper, and what cold does. This is the same sort of helper as luciferase in a firefly.
experiments.question: Which potato will make hydrogen peroxide fizz the most: a raw one, a boiled one or a very cold raw one?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which glass will have the most foam? Which will have the least? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every glass gets 3 cubes of potato of the same size, 1 centimetre on each side, the same amount of hydrogen peroxide and one drop of dish-wash liquid. You pour all the glasses at the same time and measure after the same 2 minutes. Only the potato changes: raw, boiled or cold. A fourth glass with no potato at all shows what the peroxide does alone.

materials.item: 1 bottle of hydrogen peroxide solution from a chemist, 3 percent (10 volume). If the label says 6 percent or 20 volume, a grown-up mixes it with an equal amount of water first
4 identical tall clear glasses or jars, labelled A, B, C and D with paper labels
1 raw potato, peeled, cut by a grown-up into 9 cubes of about 1 centimetre on each side
a small pan of water and a stove for a grown-up to boil 3 cubes for 5 minutes
a bowl of cold water with ice for 3 raw cubes
dish-wash liquid, 4 drops, a teaspoon, a ruler, a tray and a timer
old clothes or an apron, because peroxide can bleach cloth

experiments.safety: A grown-up does the cutting, the boiling and the pouring of the peroxide. Hydrogen peroxide is a mild chemical. Keep it off skin and out of eyes, never drink it, wash your hands afterwards and keep the bottle away from small children. If it touches skin or eyes, rinse with plenty of water. Wear old clothes, because it can bleach cloth. Do the test on a tray. Do not eat any of the potato cubes afterwards.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw each glass after 2 minutes, with the foam. Draw a bar chart of the foam heights.

setup.art: A grown-up cutting a peeled potato into small cubes on a board, and a child laying out four labelled glasses on a tray.
setup.caption: 1. Cut a potato into 9 small cubes. Set out four glasses, A to D.

setup.art: Three cubes in a pan of boiling water, and three more in a bowl of ice water, with three raw cubes waiting on a plate.
setup.caption: 2. Boil 3 cubes for 5 minutes. Chill 3 cubes in ice water. Keep 3 raw.

setup.art: A grown-up pouring a small amount of peroxide into four glasses with a drop of dish-wash liquid in each, while a child watches with a timer.
setup.caption: 3. Put the potato into the glasses. Pour the peroxide into all four at the same time.

setup.art: A child holding a ruler against the outside of a tall glass full of foam, with the other glasses beside it showing less foam.
setup.caption: 4. After 2 minutes, measure the foam height in each glass.

flow.do: Show your child the potato, the peroxide and the four glasses. Say what will go into each glass. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess down.
flow.say: We will drop potato cubes into hydrogen peroxide. Glass A gets raw potato. Glass B gets boiled potato. Glass C gets raw potato that was very cold. Glass D gets no potato. Which glass will have the most foam? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: There are four glasses: raw potato, boiled potato, cold potato and no potato. Which makes the most foam? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think boiling might change what a potato does?
good: Boiling cooks it, and cooked things are different.
Boiling kills it.
The heat might break something inside.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Do not say yet what the potato holds.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Helper That Heat Stops test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up peels the potato and cuts 9 cubes of about 1 centimetre. Boil 3 cubes for 5 minutes, then cool them under cold tap water. Put 3 cubes in a bowl of ice water for 15 minutes. Keep 3 cubes raw on a plate. Meanwhile, label the glasses A to D and put 1 drop of dish-wash liquid in each.
flow.say: While the boiled cubes cook, and the cold ones chill, we get the glasses ready. Each glass gets one drop of dish-wash liquid. The soap will help us see the bubbles as foam.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut and boil. Label the glasses A to D. Add 1 drop of soap to each.
flow.parent: While waiting for the cubes to cook and chill, your child can draw the results table and write the guess. A boiled cube must be cooled before it touches the peroxide. The cold cubes must be cold but not frozen. If you have no ice, use the coldest water from the fridge.

check.q: Why does glass D, with no potato, matter in this test?
options: It shows what the peroxide does on its own
It is a spare glass
It makes the test faster
check.why: Glass D is the control. If glass D also foamed, then the foam would not come from the potato. Picking 'a spare glass' misses that a control has a job. Picking 'faster' misses that tests are about being fair, not about being quick.

flow.context: In this step, you get the potato cubes and the glasses ready. A grown-up helps with the knife and the hot water.

flow.do: Put 3 raw cubes in glass A. Put 3 boiled cubes in glass B. Put 3 cold cubes in glass C. Leave glass D empty. Put the glasses on the tray in a row. Check the peroxide strength on the label.
flow.say: Raw in A. Boiled in B. Cold in C. Nothing in D. Look at the cubes. Do they look different? Be ready with the timer. A grown-up will pour.
flow.kid: Put the cubes in A, B and C. Nothing in D. Get the timer ready.
flow.parent: Check the label: it should say 3 percent or 10 volume. If it says 6 percent or 20 volume, mix it with an equal amount of water first. Peroxide that has stood open for a year or more may be weak.
flow.context: In this step, you put the cubes in the glasses. The peroxide goes in next.

flow.do: A grown-up pours 4 teaspoons, about 20 millilitres, of peroxide into each glass, as close to the same time as possible. Start the timer. Watch. At 2 minutes, measure the foam height with the ruler from the outside of each glass. Write the numbers.
flow.say: Ready? Pour all four now. Start the timer. What do you see in each glass? Which one bubbles first? At two minutes, we measure the foam with the ruler.
flow.kid: A grown-up pours. Start the timer. Watch each glass. Measure the foam at 2 minutes.
flow.parent: Expected: glass A foams strongly and fastest. Glass B has little or no foam. Glass C foams more slowly than A. Glass D has no foam. If A does not foam at all, the peroxide may be old: buy a new bottle. If B still foams a little, the middle of the cube did not get hot enough. That is a real result, so write it down. If the foam climbs out of the glass, stop the test, wipe up, and write 'over the top'. Cold cubes warm up fast in the liquid, so the difference between glass A and glass C may be small by 2 minutes. If so, also look at the foam after 30 seconds.

check.q: The foam in glass A is made of tiny bubbles of a gas. Which gas is it?
options: Oxygen
Steam
Smoke
check.why: The enzyme in raw potato breaks hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen gas. Oxygen is the same gas that a firefly needs for a flash. Picking 'steam' misses that nothing was hot. Picking 'smoke' misses that nothing was burning.

flow.context: In this step, a grown-up pours the peroxide into all four glasses. You watch and measure the foam.

flow.do: Look at the glasses again at 5 minutes. Draw each glass with its foam. Ask your child to compare the glasses.
flow.say: Look at the four glasses now. What is the same? What is different? Which cubes still seem to be working?
flow.kid: Look again at the glasses. Draw what you see.
flow.parent: The cold cubes in glass C may start fizzing faster as they warm. That is a good thing to talk about, because it shows that cold slows the helper but does not break it.
flow.context: In this step, you look at the glasses again and draw what you see.

flow.do: Ask your child three things: what they think now, what they saw that shows it, and why they think it happened. Draw a bar chart of the foam heights.
flow.say: Let's put it together. First, what do you think now? Second, what did you see that shows it? Third, why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer. What I think: raw potato makes peroxide fizz, and heat stops it. What I saw: raw foamed the most, boiled hardly at all, cold a medium amount, and no potato did nothing. Why: raw potato holds a helper chemical, an enzyme. Heat bends the enzyme out of shape so it cannot help. Cold only slows it. In the 1880s, Raphael Dubois found that heat also stopped the helper in a glowing beetle but left the fuel unharmed. Give this last part only after your child has given their own ideas.
flow.think: A firefly's luciferase is also an enzyme. What do you think would happen to a firefly's glow in very hot water?
flow.context: In this step, you say what the foam heights show, and draw a bar chart.

experiments.title: Glow Detective: what glows under a UV torch, and what keeps glowing?
experiments.context: This is a test with a UV torch, which shines light our eyes cannot see. You find out which everyday things glow under it, and whether the glow stops the moment the torch goes off. This shows the difference between a glow that is sent back at once and a glow that is stored.
experiments.question: Which everyday things glow under a UV torch? Which of them keep glowing after the torch is switched off?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which things on the table will glow? Which will keep glowing after the torch goes off? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Test every thing in the same dark room with the same UV torch held at the same distance, about 10 centimetres, for the same count of five. Then switch the torch off and watch for another count of five. Only the thing you test changes.
results_table: Did it glow under the UV torch?
Did it keep glowing after the torch went off?

materials.item: 1 UV torch, the kind shopkeepers use to check banknotes
a sheet of plain white printer paper and a sheet of newspaper
a yellow highlighter and a blue ballpoint pen
a white cotton cloth washed with detergent, and a white cloth that has never been washed with detergent, if you have one
a green leaf, a glass of plain water, and a glass of tonic water if you have it
a glow-in-the-dark star
a dark room

experiments.safety: UV light can harm eyes. A grown-up holds the torch. Never shine it at anyone's eyes, including your own or a pet's, and never at a mirror. Keep it pointing down at the table, and do not look into the beam. Do not shine the torch on bare skin for long. Small button batteries are dangerous if swallowed, so keep them away from children under five. Do not drink the tonic water after it has been in a test.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the thing that glowed the brightest, with its colour.

setup.art: A dark table with nine items laid out in a row: paper, newspaper, highlighter line, blue pen line, cloth, leaf, water, tonic water and a glow-in-the-dark star.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out all the things on a table. Draw your guess for each.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a UV torch pointed down at a highlighter line, which glows bright yellow-green, while a child watches.
setup.caption: 2. In a dark room, shine the UV torch on each thing from 10 centimetres.

setup.art: The torch switched off, the highlighter line dark again, and the glow-in-the-dark star still faintly glowing.
setup.caption: 3. Switch the torch off. See what keeps glowing.

flow.do: Lay out the nine things on a table. Show your child the UV torch, but do not switch it on yet. Ask for a guess for each thing and a reason. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: This torch makes a light your eyes cannot see. It is called ultraviolet. We will shine it on each thing. Which will glow? Which will keep glowing when we switch the torch off? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: There are nine things on the table, and a UV torch. Which will glow? Which will keep glowing after the torch goes off? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think a light we cannot see might make some things glow?
good: The light gives them energy.
Some things change the light into another colour.
I do not know, but it might make the paint glow.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Do not switch on the torch yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Glow Detective test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Draw a line of yellow highlighter and a line of blue pen on a plain sheet of paper. Darken the room. A grown-up holds the torch pointing down. Shine it on the white paper first.
flow.say: We switch off the room light. I will hold the torch. Look at the paper. Does it glow? What colour? Next we will test the other things.
flow.kid: Draw 2 lines on paper. Darken the room. Look at the paper under the UV torch.
flow.parent: Do not worry if the torch itself looks violet. That is only a little visible light that the torch gives out. Most white paper has a chemical that glows blue-white under UV, but some paper does not. Write down what yours does.
flow.context: In this step, you draw two lines, darken the room and test the first thing.

flow.do: Test each thing in turn for a count of five. Do the highlighter line, the blue pen line, the newspaper and the washed cloth first. Then do the unwashed cloth, the leaf, the plain water, the tonic water and the glow-in-the-dark star. Write what you see in the table.
flow.say: Next thing. Hold the torch ten centimetres away. Count to five. What do you see? What colour? Write it in the table.
flow.kid: Test each thing for a count of five. Write what you see.
flow.parent: Expected. The highlighter glows bright yellow-green or pink. The blue pen does not glow. Newspaper looks dull. A cloth washed in detergent often glows blue-white. Tonic water glows blue, but only a clear drink will work. A leaf may glow a very faint red, which may be hard to see. Plain water does not glow. The star may glow a little in green while the torch is on. Results can vary, so write what really happens.

check.q: The highlighter line glows under the UV torch. What is the torch doing?
options: Giving the highlighter light that it turns into visible light
Heating the highlighter until it glows
Shining visible light that bounces back
check.why: The torch shines UV light that our eyes cannot see. The highlighter takes in that energy and sends out visible light at the same moment. That is fluorescence. Picking 'heating' misses that the torch is cool. Picking 'bounces back' misses that UV is invisible, so a bounce would show nothing.

flow.context: In this step, you test each thing under the UV torch. You write down what you see.

flow.do: Switch the torch off. Count to five in the dark. Look at each thing again. Write which ones are still glowing. The glow-in-the-dark star should still be glowing a little.
flow.say: Now the torch is off. Look carefully. Which things are still glowing? Which went dark at once?
flow.kid: Switch the torch off. Which things still glow? Which went dark?
flow.parent: The highlighter and the cloth go dark at once, which is fluorescence. The star keeps glowing for a while, which is a stored glow. If the star does not glow, hold the torch on it for 20 seconds first. UV charges a star much better than a white torch.

check.q: The highlighter went dark the moment the torch was switched off, and the star kept glowing. What is the difference?
options: The star stored light, and the highlighter sent light back at once
The star is warmer than the highlighter
The highlighter ran out of paint
check.why: A glow that stops at once is fluorescence. A glow that carries on is stored light. Picking 'warmer' misses that neither is warm. Picking 'ran out of paint' misses that the highlighter glows again the moment the torch comes back on.

flow.context: In this step, you switch off the torch and see which things keep glowing.

flow.do: Ask your child three things: what they think now, what they saw, and why they think it happened. Then compare these glows with a firefly, who needs no torch at all.
flow.say: Let's put it together. First, what do you think now? Second, what did you see? Third, why do you think it happened? Then tell me how a firefly's glow is different from all of these.
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why it happened. Then say how a firefly is different.
flow.parent: A good answer. What I think: some things send light back at once when a UV torch shines, and some store it. What I saw: the highlighter, the cloth and the tonic water glowed and went dark when the torch was off, and the star kept glowing. Why: fluorescent things turn the invisible UV into visible light at once, and stored glows keep the light and let it out slowly. A firefly is different because they make new light from chemicals, and need no torch at all.
flow.think: Why does a banknote have parts that glow under UV, and who would want to check this?
flow.context: In this step, you say what the test showed, and compare it with living light.

activities.title: The Little Black Windows: watch your pupils change
activities.context: This is a quick look at the first thing your eyes do when light changes. The black circle in the middle of your eye is called the pupil. You watch it change size, with no torch and no tools.

materials.item: a bright room, such as a room with the lights on or a sunny window
a partner to watch, a parent or a friend
a timer or a watch with a second hand
paper and pencil

activities.safety: Never shine a torch into anyone's eyes. This activity needs only a bright room and your own hands.

schedule.what: Cover your eyes for 30 seconds. Open them and let your partner watch your pupils. Swap roles. Draw what you saw.

activities.record: Draw one eye twice: the pupil just after the hands are taken away, and the pupil two seconds later. Write whether it grew or shrank.

setup.art: A close-up drawing of an eye with a large black pupil and a small coloured ring, next to the same eye with a small pupil and a large coloured ring.
setup.caption: 1. Look at an eye. The black circle in the middle is the pupil.

setup.art: A child sitting in a bright room with both hands cupped over their eyes, and a partner waiting in front with a timer.
setup.caption: 2. Cover your eyes with your hands for 30 seconds.

setup.art: The child lowering their hands while the partner watches closely, and a small arrow showing the pupil shrinking.
setup.caption: 3. Take your hands away. Your partner watches your pupils.

flow.do: Sit facing your child in a bright room. Look at their eyes. Find the black circle in the middle. Ask them to look at yours. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: Look at my eye. The black circle in the middle is the pupil. It is a hole that lets light into the eye. Now, if I cover my eyes with my hands for a while, what do you think will happen to my pupils? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at your partner's eyes. The black circle is the pupil. Guess what happens when eyes are covered.

ask.q: Why do you think the pupil might change size?
good: In the dark it opens to let in more light.
In bright light it gets smaller so it does not hurt.
It does not change.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. If the eye colour is dark brown, the pupil is hard to see. Stand near a window, or choose someone whose eyes are lighter.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Little Black Windows activity. You find the pupil and guess what it will do.

flow.do: Your child covers their eyes with cupped hands for 30 seconds. The room stays bright. Then they take their hands away. You watch their pupils closely for the first three seconds. Say what you saw.
flow.say: Cover your eyes with both hands, like a tent. Keep your eyes open under your hands. I will count thirty seconds. Now take your hands away. I am watching your pupils.
flow.kid: Cover your eyes with cupped hands for 30 seconds. Take your hands away. Your partner watches.
flow.parent: Expected: just after the hands move, the pupils are wide, and within about two seconds they shrink. It can be quick, so repeat the test two or three times. Keep the room just as bright each time.

check.q: When hands are taken away from the eyes in a bright room, what happens to the pupils?
options: They start wide and then get smaller
They start small and then get wider
They stay the same size
check.why: Under the hands, it was dark, so the pupils opened wide to let in more light. In bright light they shrink so less light gets in. Picking 'stay the same' misses that pupils change in about a second or two.

flow.context: In this step, you cover your eyes and then watch the pupils shrink.

flow.do: Swap roles. Now you cover your eyes, and your child watches your pupils. Then draw one eye twice: the pupil just after the hands moved, and the pupil two seconds later.
flow.say: Now it is my turn. I will cover my eyes. You watch my pupils when I take my hands away. Then draw one eye twice, once big and once small.
flow.kid: Swap. Watch your partner's pupils. Draw one eye twice.
flow.context: In this step, you swap roles and draw what you saw.

flow.do: Ask your child three things: what they think now, what they saw, and why they think pupils change. Then mention that cat pupils are slits and an octopus has a rectangular pupil.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think pupils change? A cat's pupil is a thin slit by day and a big circle at night. Why might that help a cat?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer. What I think: pupils get bigger in the dark and smaller in bright light. What I saw: the black circle shrank in about two seconds. Why: the pupil lets light in, so a bigger pupil catches more light in the dark. Pupils can change the amount of light by roughly ten times or more, but the chemical change in the retina is a much bigger change. That takes about twenty minutes, as you will see in the Eyes in the Dark test.
flow.think: A firefly's flash is faint. What could an owl do with their pupils to see it better?
flow.context: In this step, you say what you saw about pupils, and compare with a cat.

activities.title: Look Beside It: a glow seen from the corner of the eye
activities.context: This is a test of where in your eye a faint light is easiest to see. You look straight at a hidden glow, and then a little to one side, and compare. Do it right after the Eyes in the Dark test, or after 15 minutes in the dark.

materials.item: the glow stick, the 12 half-sheets of paper, the table and chair from the Eyes in the Dark test
a small piece of tape
a completely dark room
a pad and pencil

activities.safety: Stay in the room with your child. Clear the floor. Never cut or bite a glow stick.

schedule.what: Sit in the dark until your eyes are ready. Find the glow by looking straight at it. Then find it by looking beside it. Compare how many sheets you can see it through.

activities.record: Write the number of sheets left on top when you first saw the glow, looking straight at it, and looking beside it.

setup.art: A stack of paper sheets over a glow stick, with a small piece of tape stuck on the table 10 centimetres to the left.
setup.caption: 1. Stick a piece of tape on the table, 10 centimetres to the side of the stack.

setup.art: A child with eyes pointing at the centre of the stack, a dotted line from the eye to the stack.
setup.caption: 2. Look straight at the middle of the stack. Lift sheets until you see the glow.

setup.art: A child with eyes pointing at the tape mark, with the stack just visible at the edge of their view.
setup.caption: 3. Look at the tape mark. Lift sheets until you see the glow from the corner of your eye.

flow.do: Sit in the dark room with your child for at least 15 minutes first. Or do this straight after the Eyes in the Dark test. Stick a small piece of tape on the table 10 centimetres to the left of the stack. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: We will look for a glow in two ways. First, we look straight at the middle of the stack. Second, we look at the tape, and use the corner of our eye. Which do you think will let you see the glow through more sheets? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look straight at the stack, then at the tape beside it. Which shows the glow better? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think looking at one place might be better than another?
good: Looking straight is better because you point your eye at it.
The corner of my eye might see better in the dark.
Maybe there is no difference.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many people expect that looking straight at a thing is best. In dim light, it is often the opposite.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Look Beside It test. You guess where your eye sees best.

flow.do: Put all 12 sheets over the glow stick. Your child looks straight at the middle of the stack. They lift off sheets one by one until they see the glow. Count the sheets left. Write the number. Put the sheets back.
flow.say: Look straight at the middle of the stack. Lift off one sheet at a time. Say stop when you first see the glow. We count the sheets left.
flow.kid: Look straight at the stack. Lift off sheets until you see the glow. Count the sheets left.
flow.parent: Make sure that your child keeps their eyes pointed at the middle of the stack, and not wandering. Ask them to say where they are looking.
flow.context: In this step, you look straight at the stack and count the sheets.

flow.do: Put all 12 sheets back. This time your child looks at the tape mark. They keep their eyes on the tape and lift off sheets one by one. They stop when they see the glow in the corner of the eye. Count the sheets left. Write the number.
flow.say: Now look at the tape, not at the stack. Keep your eyes on the tape. Lift off the sheets one at a time. Say stop when you see a glow in the corner of your eye.
flow.kid: Look at the tape, not the stack. Lift off sheets. Count the sheets left when you see the glow.
flow.parent: Looking beside the stack often lets people see the glow through one or two more sheets, but not always. If your child sees no difference, write that down. It is a real result. Try the tape on the other side too.

check.q: Your child sees the glow through more sheets when looking beside it than when looking straight at it. What is the best explanation?
options: The middle of the retina has few rod cells, and the sides have many
The glow is brighter at the sides
The paper is thinner at the sides
check.why: The very centre of your retina is packed with cone cells, which need bright light. The areas around it have many more rod cells, which work in dim light. Picking 'brighter at the sides' misses that the stick did not move. Picking 'thinner paper' misses that the sheets were the same for both tests.

flow.context: In this step, you look beside the stack and count the sheets.

flow.do: Compare the two numbers. Ask your child three things: what they think now, what numbers they got, and why they think it happened. Mention that astronomers use this trick to see faint stars.
flow.say: What do you think now? What numbers did you get? Why do you think the corner of the eye might see a faint light better? Astronomers use this trick to look at faint stars. They call it averted vision.
flow.kid: Compare your two numbers. Say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer. What I think: a faint light is easier to see from the corner of the eye. What I saw: I saw the glow through more sheets when I looked beside it. Why: the middle of the eye has cone cells, which need bright light, and the sides have many rod cells.
flow.context: In this step, you compare the two numbers and say what they show.

activities.title: The Crowd and the Signal: why bacteria glow only in a crowd
activities.context: This is a model of how glowing bacteria count each other. A spoonful of coloured water stands for the signal chemical that one bacterium makes. A glass stands for a squid's tiny light organ, and a big jug stands for the open sea. You count how much signal you need to make the water look coloured.

materials.item: food colouring, 5 drops, or a strong tea decoction
half a cup of water for the coloured signal water
1 small glass holding about 200 millilitres of clear water
1 jug or pot holding about 2 litres of clear water
a tablespoon, a sheet of white paper and a marker for tally marks
one more glass of plain water to compare with

activities.safety: Food colour can stain clothes and hands. Do the test on a tray. Do not drink the coloured water.

schedule.what: Make the signal water. Add spoonfuls to the glass until it looks coloured. Add spoonfuls to the jug. Compare the counts.

activities.record: Write the number of spoonfuls needed for the glass, and for the jug. Divide the jug number by the glass number.

setup.art: A half cup of water with five drops of red food colour being stirred, labelled signal water.
setup.caption: 1. Make the signal water: 5 drops of food colour in half a cup of water.

setup.art: A tablespoon of signal water being added to a small glass of clear water on a sheet of white paper, next to a plain glass.
setup.caption: 2. Add one spoonful at a time to the glass. Stop when it looks coloured.

setup.art: A large jug of clear water on white paper receiving spoonfuls of signal water, with tally marks next to it.
setup.caption: 3. Do the same with the jug. Count the spoonfuls.

flow.do: Show your child the glass, the jug and the coloured signal water. Explain that each spoonful is the signal from one bacterium. Ask for a guess: how many spoonfuls will the jug need compared with the glass?
flow.say: Each spoonful of coloured water is the signal that one bacterium makes. The glass is like a squid's tiny light organ. The jug is like the open sea. When the water looks coloured, the bacteria know the crowd is big enough. How many spoonfuls will the glass need? And the jug? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A spoonful of coloured water is one bacterium's signal. How many spoonfuls will the glass need? How many will the jug need? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the jug will need more or fewer spoonfuls than the glass?
good: The jug is bigger, so the colour spreads out more.
It will need the same, because it is the same colour.
The jug will need a lot more.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Crowd and the Signal activity. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Stir 5 drops of food colour into half a cup of water. This is the signal water. Put the small glass of water and a second glass of plain water side by side on the white paper. You will compare them by looking from above.
flow.say: This is the signal water. We will add it one spoonful at a time. We stop when the water in the glass looks clearly different from the plain glass.
flow.kid: Stir 5 drops of colour into half a cup of water. Put 2 glasses on white paper.
flow.context: In this step, you make the signal water and set out the glasses.

flow.do: Add one spoonful of signal water to the small glass. Stir. Compare it with the plain glass. Keep going, one spoonful at a time, until it looks clearly coloured. Make a tally mark for each spoonful.
flow.say: One spoonful in. Stir. Does it look coloured? Compare with the plain glass. If not, add another. Count every spoonful.
flow.kid: Add a spoonful to the glass. Stir. Does it look coloured? Make a tally mark.

check.q: In this model, why is a small glass like a squid's light organ?
options: The signal builds up quickly in a small space
The glass is made of glass
The glass glows
check.why: In a small space, each bit of signal stays close and the level goes up fast. In the open sea, the signal drifts away. Picking 'the glass glows' mixes up the model with the real bacteria.

flow.context: In this step, you add signal water to the small glass and count how many spoonfuls it needs.

flow.do: Now do the same with the jug. Add one spoonful at a time, stir, compare with a plain glass of the same water, and tally. Stop when the jug looks clearly coloured, or at 30 spoonfuls.
flow.say: Now the jug. It holds about ten times as much water. Add a spoonful, stir, and look. How many spoonfuls will it take? Let's keep counting.
flow.kid: Do the same with the jug. Add spoonfuls. Count them.
flow.parent: Expected: the glass needs about one or two spoonfuls, and the 2-litre jug about ten times as many, which may be 10 to 20. The exact number depends on your colour and your eyes. If the jug is not coloured after 30 spoonfuls, make the signal water stronger and try again. Write the real numbers.
flow.context: In this step, you do the same test with the big jug and count the spoonfuls.

flow.do: Divide the jug count by the glass count. Ask your child three things: what they think now, what they saw, and why they think it happened.
flow.say: How many more spoonfuls did the jug need? What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think a glowing bacterium alone in the sea stays dark?
flow.kid: Compare the two counts. Say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer. What I think: a signal is strong only if there are many bacteria in a small space. What I saw: the glass needed a few spoonfuls and the jug needed many more. Why: in the big jug the signal spreads out. That is why bacteria in the open sea stay dark and bacteria packed in a squid's light organ glow.
flow.think: A squid empties out most of their bacteria at dawn. What would happen to the signal inside their light organ then?
flow.context: In this step, you compare the counts and say what they show about glowing bacteria.

activities.title: Colours Go to Sleep: can you name colours in very dim light?
activities.context: This is a test of the two kinds of light catchers in your eye. Cone cells see colour in bright light. Rod cells work in dim light and see no colour. You try to name the colours of paper squares in a very dim light, after waiting in the dark.

materials.item: 6 squares of coloured paper, each about 5 centimetres wide: red, green, blue, yellow, white and black
a tray or a plain cloth to put them on
a phone with a torch, and 8 or more sheets of white printer paper
a completely dark room, a timer and a pad

activities.safety: Stay in the room with your child. Clear the floor. Do not shine the torch into anyone's eyes.

schedule.what: Put the squares in a row. Wait in the dark for 15 minutes. Use a very dim light made of a phone torch under sheets of paper. Try to name the colours. Then add light and check.

activities.record: Write what you called each square in the dim light, and what colour it really was.

setup.art: Six squares of coloured paper in a row on a tray, each with a small number written on the back.
setup.caption: 1. Number the squares on the back. Mix up their order on the tray.

setup.art: A phone torch lying face up on a table under a stack of white sheets, lighting the squares very dimly from a distance of one metre.
setup.caption: 2. Make a very dim light: put a phone torch under a stack of white sheets.

setup.art: A child squinting at six grey-looking squares in a dim room, with a few faint colours showing.
setup.caption: 3. After 15 minutes in the dark, name the colour of each square.

flow.do: Number the squares on the back and mix up their order. Lay them in a row on a tray, 1 metre from where your child will sit. Ask for a guess: will they be able to name the colours in a very dim light?
flow.say: Here are six paper squares of different colours. Soon we will put out the lights and make a very dim light. Do you think you will be able to name every colour? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Six coloured squares. In very dim light, can you name every colour? Why?

ask.q: Why might colours look different in very dim light?
good: There is not enough light to see the colour.
Colours look grey at night.
I will see all colours as usual.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Make sure your child does not see the order of the squares before the test.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Colours Go to Sleep activity. You set out the squares and guess.

flow.do: Make a very dim light. Switch on a phone torch and put it face up on a table behind the squares. Cover it with 8 sheets of white paper. Switch off the room light. Check from your seat that you can just see the squares as shapes.
flow.say: The torch is under the sheets, so the light is very dim. If you can see every colour clearly, add more sheets. If you cannot see the squares at all, take off a sheet.
flow.kid: Cover the phone torch with 8 sheets. Switch off the room light. Add or remove sheets until you just see the squares.
flow.parent: The light must be dim enough that the squares look like shapes, but not so dim that they vanish. This may take a few tries. If your phone is bright, you may need 15 sheets or more.
flow.context: In this step, you make a very dim light and set the right brightness.

flow.do: Wait in the dark for 15 minutes. Do not use any other light. Tell a story or sing quietly. Then your child names the colours of the squares from left to right. You write down what they say.
flow.say: We have waited in the dark. Now look at the squares one at a time. Say what colour you think each one is. It is fine to guess. I will write down what you say.
flow.kid: Wait in the dark. Then name the colour of each square, left to right.
flow.parent: Expected: many people see the squares as greys. Often the white square looks brightest, the black darkest, and red looks dark. Blue and green may look lighter than red. Some people can name some colours. If your child can name every colour easily, add more sheets and try again. Write what really happens.

check.q: In very dim light, why are colours hard to name?
options: Rod cells work in dim light but cannot tell colours
Colours are only in the paper in the daytime
The eye gets tired of colours
check.why: In dim light, the cone cells that see colour do not catch enough light, and the rod cells take over. Rod cells cannot tell colours apart. Picking 'only in the daytime' mixes up the paper with the eye. The paper does not change.

flow.context: In this step, you wait in the dark and try to name the colours.

flow.do: Turn on the room light and check each square. Count how many your child named correctly. Ask your child three things: what they think now, what they saw, and why they think it happened.
flow.say: Now the light is on. Let's check. How many did you name correctly? What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think colours seem to fade in the dark?
flow.kid: Switch on the light. Check each square. Count how many you got right. Say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer. What I think: colours fade in very dim light. What I saw: I called the squares greys, and only the white and black were easy. Why: rod cells work in dim light but cannot see colour, and cone cells need more light. It is also why a moonlit garden looks grey.
flow.context: In this step, you check the colours and say what the test showed.

projects.title: How Dark Is Our Sky? A star count in three conditions
projects.context: This is a star count. You count how many stars you can see in a fixed patch of the sky, on three nights with different amounts of light and waiting. You find out how bright lights, and eyes that have not waited in the dark, change the number of stars you can see.

materials.item: a piece of card about 25 centimetres square with a 15 centimetre square window cut out by a grown-up
a piece of string 60 centimetres long
a notebook and pencil, and a dim torch with red cloth over it
a balcony, terrace, window or open space with a view of the sky straight overhead

projects.safety: Go outside only with a grown-up. Stay on the balcony, terrace or a safe open space. Keep the red torch dim and never point it at anyone's eyes.

schedule.what: Make the card window. Go out with all the lights on. Count the stars straight overhead straight away, without waiting. Write the number.
Switch off the lights near you. Wait 20 minutes in the dark. Count the stars again. Write the number.
Count again from a darker place, or very late at night when more lights are off. Make a bar chart of the three counts and write a short report.

projects.record: Each night write the date, the time, the place, the weather and the number of stars. On night 3, draw a bar chart.

setup.art: A square piece of card with a square window cut out, and a string tied to a corner for a child to hold against their nose.
setup.caption: 1. Make a card with a window, and a string to hold at arm's length.

setup.art: A child on a balcony at night holding the card at the end of a string up to the sky, and counting stars through the window.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the string to your nose. Look straight up through the window and count stars.

setup.art: Three bars of different heights labelled lights on, lights off and wait 20 minutes, and darker place.
setup.caption: 3. Draw a bar chart of the three counts.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts a 15 centimetre square window in the card. Tie a 60 centimetre string to one corner. Ask your child to guess how many stars they will count in the window on the three nights, and why.
flow.say: This card is our window on the sky. When we hold the string to our nose and look up, the window always shows the same patch. How many stars do you think we will see tonight with the lights on? And after waiting in the dark? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Make a card with a window. Hold the string to your nose. Guess how many stars you will see.

ask.q: What might change the number of stars you can see on different nights?
good: Clouds.
Bright lights nearby.
How long my eyes have been in the dark.

flow.parent: Choose nights with a clear sky and, if you can, no bright Moon. Count at the same time of night each time. A Moon in the sky hides faint stars, so write down if it is out.
flow.context: This is the first step of the star count. You make the card and guess.

flow.do: On night 1, keep all the lights on near you. Go out. Hold the string against your nose and the card out straight. Look straight up through the window. Count the stars in the window. Write the number, and anything else you notice.
flow.say: Night one. All our lights are on. Hold the string to your nose and look straight up through the window. Count every star you can see. Write down the number.
flow.kid: Hold the string to your nose. Look straight up. Count the stars in the window.
flow.parent: A planet looks like a star, so count it too and write that it may be a planet. If the number is zero, write zero. A zero is a real result.
flow.context: In this step, you do the first star count with all the lights on.

flow.do: On night 2, switch off as many lights near you as you safely can. Wait 20 minutes outside or by an open window, with your eyes open. Do not look at your phone. Then count the stars in the window again. Write the number.
flow.say: Night two. We have put out the lights. We wait twenty minutes, and then we count. What do you think the number will be this time?
flow.kid: Lights off. Wait 20 minutes. Do not look at a phone. Count the stars again.
flow.wait: Do this on the second night

check.q: On night 2, you see more stars than on night 1, though the sky is the same. What are the best reasons?
options: Your eyes got used to the dark, and there were fewer bright lights around
More stars came out
The card window got bigger
check.why: Waiting makes the rod cells ready, and switching off lamps makes the sky darker around you. The stars were there all along. Picking 'more stars came out' misses that stars do not switch on at night. Picking 'the window got bigger' misses that the string keeps the window the same size.

flow.context: In this step, you wait in the dark for 20 minutes and count the stars again on night 2.

flow.do: On night 3, count from a darker place if you can, such as a village or a dark terrace. Or count later at night, when more lights are off. Wait 20 minutes first. Count the stars in the window. Write the number.
flow.say: Night three. We are in the darkest place we can find. We wait twenty minutes and then count. Let's see how many stars the window holds.
flow.kid: Go to a darker place. Wait 20 minutes. Count the stars.
flow.wait: Do this on the third night
flow.parent: A dark place may be a relative's village, a hill or a field outside the city. If you cannot get to one, choose the darkest hour you can, with the fewest lights on. Write what you did.
flow.context: In this step, you do the third count from a darker place.

flow.do: Draw a bar chart with three bars. Write a short report: where, when, what you counted and what you think.
flow.say: Let's draw a bar for each night. Which night had the most stars? What was different on that night? Now write a short report. What do you think, what did you count, and why?
flow.kid: Draw 3 bars. Which night had the most stars? Why? Write a short report.
flow.parent: A good report. Light from lamps and buildings makes the sky glow, so faint stars cannot be seen. In a village far from lights, hundreds of stars can be seen. Many astronomers around the world use star counts like this one to measure light pollution.
flow.think: Where would you go in your state to see the most stars, and who could tell you?
flow.context: In this step, you draw a bar chart of your counts and write a short report.

challenges.title: The Unforgeable Flash: invent a signal that a trickster cannot copy
challenges.context: In the first Living light unit, you read about trickster fireflies, who copy the answer flash of another kind of firefly to catch them. This is a design challenge. You invent a flash code for two friends. A trickster watches and tries to copy it, and your code must still work.
challenges.problem: You and a friend are on opposite sides of a dark room. You each have a torch. Invent a flash code so you know it is really your friend, and not a trickster who has been watching and copying. The trickster gets to watch your code three times.
constraints: You may use only torches, with no sound and no words.
The code must work in a dim room, and nobody may shine a torch in anyone's eyes.
The trickster is a family member who watches three rounds and then tries to copy the code.
The code must be easy for the two friends to remember.
materials: red, green or blue cellophane, if you have it
a watch or phone with a second hand
general: A pattern of long and short flashes, like 1 long, 2 short, followed by a reply from your friend after a wait.
A first flash and a reply, with the wait between them set to exactly 2 seconds.
A password flash that you change on every night.
creative: Make the code change after every flash, so a copy of the last round does not work on the next.
Add a colour change with a piece of cellophane over the torch that only you two know about.
Make the length of the wait the secret. A trickster can copy a flash, but it is hard to copy a wait of exactly two heartbeats.
challenges.your_turn: Invent your own code. Write it down. Test it with a trickster who watches three rounds. Change one thing and test again. Which code was hardest to copy? Why do you think so?

setup.art: Two children facing each other in a dim room, each holding a torch, and a third child sitting to the side watching.
setup.caption: 1. Two friends and a trickster. The friends have a torch each.

setup.art: A paper with a drawn code: long and short dashes and a clock showing a 2 second wait.
setup.caption: 2. Write the code down: the flashes, the wait and the reply.

setup.art: The trickster copying the flash with a third torch, while the friend shakes their head.
setup.caption: 3. The trickster tries to copy the code. Does the friend notice?

flow.do: Read the problem together. Explain the trickster fireflies. Ask for ideas on what a trickster could copy easily and what would be hard to copy.
flow.say: Some female fireflies copy the answer flash of another kind of firefly, and then catch the males who come. Our trickster is a person who watches and copies. What is easy to copy about a flash? What is hard?
flow.kid: A trickster watches your flashes. What is easy to copy? What is hard to copy?

ask.q: What part of a flash code would be hardest to copy?
good: A secret that is not in the flash.
The exact time between flashes.
A change that happens every time.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Unforgeable Flash challenge. You think about what a trickster can copy.

flow.do: Your child and a friend, or your child and you, design a code and write it down. They decide the flashes, the wait before the reply, and what the reply is.
flow.say: Design your code. How many flashes? How long between them? What does your friend send back? Write it down so you both remember it.
flow.kid: Design a code. Write down the flashes, the wait and the reply.
flow.context: In this step, you design and write down the flash code.

flow.do: In a dim room, the two friends use the code three times. The trickster watches. Then the trickster tries to copy it. The friend says if they believe the trickster. Write down whether it worked.
flow.say: Trickster, watch carefully. Friends, send your code three times. Now trickster, your turn. Friend, is that your real friend, or the trickster?
flow.kid: Use your code 3 times. The trickster tries to copy it. Is your friend fooled?

check.q: A code is just three quick flashes with no reply. Why is it easy for a trickster to copy?
options: Everything about it is visible, so the trickster can copy all of it
Three flashes is too many
Flashes cannot be copied
check.why: A trickster copies what they can see. A secret that is not in the flash, such as a hidden change or an exact wait, is harder to copy. Picking 'flashes cannot be copied' misses that the trickster fireflies really do copy flashes.

flow.parent: Be a fair trickster. Copy the flashes as well as you can, and do not guess at a secret. If you manage to copy your child's code, that is useful. It tells them what to change.
flow.context: In this step, you test the code against a trickster.

flow.do: Change one thing in the code to make it harder to copy. Test again. Compare the two codes.
flow.say: Change one thing. Make the code harder to copy. Now test again with the trickster. Which code was harder to copy, the first or the second? Why?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test again. Which code was harder to copy?
flow.think: Real fireflies cannot change their code each night. What might happen to a species whose code is copied by a trickster?
flow.context: In this step, you improve the code and test it again.

challenges.title: Fireflies in Step: invent your own rule for flashing together
challenges.context: In the Flash Together game, fireflies lined up by joining a flash they saw when they were past halfway. This is a design challenge. You invent your own rule and test whether it lines up the group faster, or not at all.
challenges.problem: Design a rule for the Flash Together game so that a group of fireflies with different beats flashes together as fast as possible. There must be no leader, and each firefly may use only their own marker and the flashes they see.
constraints: No firefly may be the leader, and nobody may tell anyone else when to flash.
A firefly may use only their own marker, their own beat, and the flashes they can see.
Your rule must fit in one sentence.
Test every rule with the same cards and the same start numbers, three times, and count the ticks.
materials: the cards, counting tracks and markers from the Flash Together game
a metronome set to 60 beats a minute, or a loud clock
paper and a pencil to write down each rule and its result
general: The game rule: flash when you see a flash and your marker is at the halfway number or further.
A shyer rule: join only if your marker is at least one third of the way to your number.
A bolder rule: join any flash you see, whatever your marker says.
creative: A rule where you move your marker forward by 2 boxes whenever you see a flash, but never flash early. Test whether this works.
A very shy rule: join only if your marker is one box from your own flash number. Test whether this works.
A rule that joins a flash only when two or more fireflies flash together, as if the louder the crowd, the more you listen.
challenges.your_turn: Make up a rule. Write it in one sentence. Test it three times with the same cards. Count the ticks each time, and count how many rounds worked at all. Which rule lined the group up fastest? Which rule failed? Why do you think so?

setup.art: Four children with markers on counting tracks, each standing ready to flash, and a paper with a rule written on it.
setup.caption: 1. Write your rule in one sentence.

setup.art: The same four children flashing together after a few ticks, while a parent writes a tally of ticks.
setup.caption: 2. Test the rule three times with the same cards. Count the ticks.

setup.art: A table comparing three rules by number of ticks, with one rule marked never.
setup.caption: 3. Compare the rules in a table. Which was fastest? Which never worked?

flow.do: Read the problem together. Recall the listen rule from the Flash Together game, and how many ticks the group took to line up. Ask your child to guess how to make a rule that is faster.
flow.say: In the game, we lined up after about a dozen ticks. Can you make a rule that is faster? Can you make one that fails? Think of a rule, and write it in one sentence.
flow.kid: Think of a new rule. Could it be faster than the game rule? Write it in one sentence.

ask.q: What would make a group line up faster?
good: Joining a flash sooner.
Joining every flash I see.
Moving closer to the flash.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Fireflies in Step challenge. You think of a rule and write it down.

flow.do: Choose three rules to test: the game rule, your child's own rule and one more rule. Write each in one sentence. Fix the cards and start numbers, so each rule is tested the same way.
flow.say: We test three rules. The game rule, your rule, and one more. We use the same cards and the same start numbers for each. Why is that important?
flow.kid: Pick 3 rules. Use the same cards and start numbers for each. Why is that fair?

check.q: Why must every rule be tested with the same cards and start numbers?
options: So only the rule changes, and the result comes from the rule
So the game takes longer
So nobody wins
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If the cards changed too, a rule might look faster only because of an easy start.

flow.context: In this step, you choose the rules to test and fix the cards and start numbers.

flow.do: Test each rule three times. For each round, count the ticks until everyone flashes together twice in a row, or stop at 40. Write each result in a table.
flow.say: Rule one, round one. Start the beat. Everyone follows the rule. Count the ticks until we flash together twice in a row.
flow.kid: Test each rule 3 times. Count the ticks. Stop at 40.
flow.parent: Results from computer tests of the same game. A rule that says join if your marker is at the halfway number or further lines the group up in at most about 19 ticks. A bolder rule that joins any flash is faster, up to about 14 ticks. A very shy rule that joins only one box before your own number never lines up in 40 ticks. A rule that only moves your marker forward 1, 2 or 3 boxes and never joins did not line up either. Real players may be slower than the computer, because people make mistakes in counting.
flow.context: In this step, you test each rule three times and count the ticks.

flow.do: Compare the three rules in a table. Ask which was fastest and which failed. Then ask your child three things: what they think now, what they saw, and why they think the best rule worked.
flow.say: Which rule was fastest? Which never worked? What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think the best rule worked?
flow.kid: Which rule was fastest? Which failed? Say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer. What I think: the more willing each firefly is to join, the faster the group lines up. What I saw: the bold rule was fastest, and the shy rule never worked. Why: joining a flash pulls fireflies into step, and a rule that joins too late or only nudges never makes them flash at the same tick.
flow.think: A firefly that joins every flash flashes at the pace of the fastest one. Is that good or bad for the group?
flow.context: In this step, you compare the rules and say which worked and why.

videos.title: How fireflies flash together in step
videos.why: To see thousands of fireflies flashing together in a tree, as in the mangroves of Southeast Asia.
videos.check: Not yet found. Find a short film from a science channel, watch it, and check that it is accurate before adding it.

videos.title: Why your eyes need time to see in the dark
videos.why: To see how rod cells, cone cells and rhodopsin let your eyes adapt to dim light.
videos.check: Not yet found. Find one, watch it, and check that it explains dark adaptation correctly before adding it.

videos.title: The squid and the glowing bacteria
videos.why: To see the Hawaiian bobtail squid, and hear how a squid and glowing bacteria share one lamp.
videos.check: Not yet found. Find one, watch it, and check that it is accurate before adding it.

quiz.p: A test tube holding firefly luciferin, luciferase and oxygen glows for a short while and then fades. What brings the glow back?
opts: ATP
Switching on a torch
Cooling the tube
quiz.why: A flash needs a payment of cell energy. ATP is the energy carrier, and adding it brings the glow back. A torch would not help, because a firefly makes new light and does not store old light. Cooling would only slow the reaction.

quiz.p: When milk is boiled, many of the enzymes in the milk stop working. Why?
opts: Heat bends the enzymes out of shape, so they cannot grip anything
Heat uses the enzymes up
Heat adds water to the enzymes
quiz.why: An enzyme works by its shape. Strong heat bends the shape and the enzyme stops working. It is not used up. Even before boiling, an enzyme is never used up when it does its job.

quiz.p: What happens to an enzyme after it has helped with one reaction?
opts: It is free to help with the same reaction again
It is used up
It turns into light
quiz.why: Enzymes are not used up. A single enzyme can do the same job thousands of times in a second. Picking 'turns into light' mixes up the enzyme luciferase with luciferin, which is the chemical that gives out the light.

quiz.p: A thing glows under a UV torch and goes dark at the moment the torch is switched off. What kind of glow is it?
opts: Fluorescence
Phosphorescence
Living light
quiz.why: A glow that stops at once when the light stops is fluorescence. A stored glow would fade slowly. Living light would carry on in total darkness, with no torch at all.

quiz.p: A white shirt glows blue-white under a UV lamp. A friend says the shirt is bioluminescent. What is wrong with that?
opts: The shirt is not alive, and it needs the UV lamp to glow
Shirts cannot glow at all
The glow is stored light
quiz.why: Bioluminescence is light made by living beings, and it carries on with no other light. The shirt glows only while the lamp is on, so it is fluorescence. Picking 'stored light' mixes up two kinds of glow. A stored glow would linger after the lamp goes off.

quiz.p: Why does a hatchetfish make blue belly lights?
opts: Blue matches the faint light from above, so their shadow disappears
Blue is the warmest colour
Blue lights are the brightest lights
quiz.why: The light that comes down to the deep sea is a faint blue, because blue goes furthest in water. Belly lights of the same colour and brightness hide a dark shape from hunters below. Picking 'warmest' misses that living light is cold.

quiz.p: You step from bright sunshine into a dark room and cannot see the chairs. A minute later you can see a little, and after twenty minutes you see a lot. What is the best explanation?
opts: Your eyes slowly get ready, as rod cells build back their light-catching chemical
The chairs slowly become brighter
The room slowly gets lighter
quiz.why: Nothing in the room changed. Bright light had used up the rhodopsin in your rod cells, and in the dark it is slowly built back. Picking 'the room gets lighter' misses that a dark room has no new light coming in.

quiz.p: Faint stars seem to vanish when you stare straight at them, and come back when you look a little to one side. Why?
opts: The centre of the retina has few rod cells, and the sides have many
Stars move when you look at them
Your pupils close when you stare
quiz.why: Rod cells catch faint light, and there are few in the very centre of the retina. Looking a little to the side puts the star's light on more rods. Picking 'stars move' misses that stars stay where they are.

quiz.p: The sea is huge and a squid's light organ is tiny. How does this help the glowing bacteria count themselves?
opts: In the tiny organ the signal chemical builds up, and in the sea it spreads out and fades
The sea is too cold for bacteria to glow
The squid tells the bacteria when to glow
quiz.why: Bacteria switch on their light when their signal chemical passes a level. In a small, crowded space, it builds up fast. In the open sea, it drifts away. Picking 'the squid tells them' misses that the bacteria answer a chemical signal from each other.

quiz.p: A newborn bobtail squid has no glowing bacteria. How do they get them?
opts: They pick them up from the sea water
They are born with them
They get them from their mother's food
quiz.why: A baby squid has no bacteria at first. They pick up the right kind from the sea water, and only one kind is allowed to stay. Picking 'born with them' misses that this partnership has to be set up again by each new squid.

quiz.p: There are two groups of fireflies with different beats. In group one, each firefly joins any flash they see once they are past halfway to their own flash. In group two, each firefly ignores every flash but their own. Which group will line up, and why?
opts: Group one, because answering each other's flashes pulls them into step
Group two, because each keeps their own steady beat
Neither, because only a leader can line them up
quiz.why: A firefly that joins a flash when they are past halfway pulls late fireflies into step, and after a few cycles the group flashes together. A group that ignores all flashes keeps its different beats and almost never lines up. Picking 'only a leader' misses what this unit shows: no leader is needed.

quiz.p: The pacemaker cells of your heart keep time together with no boss cell. How is this like fireflies flashing together?
opts: Each cell answers its neighbours, and the whole group keeps one beat
Both are led by one main cell
Both make light
quiz.why: In both cases, many separate beats pull each other into step. No member leads. Picking 'one main cell' misses what this unit shows: no leader is needed.

quiz.p: A scientist adds the gene for a green glowing protein next to the gene for a nerve cell's protein. What does the green glow tell her?
opts: That the nerve cell's gene is working in that cell
That the cell is hot
That the cell is dead
quiz.why: The glowing gene is switched on wherever the gene beside it is switched on. So the green light marks where the gene is working. Picking 'hot' misses that this glow is cold.

quiz.p: Why is a bright lamp near a beach bad for baby turtles?
opts: They crawl towards the brightest horizon, so they may crawl away from the sea
The lamp makes the sea warm
The lamp makes the sand too hot
quiz.why: Hatchlings use the brightest, lowest horizon to find the sea. A lamp behind the beach can pull them the wrong way. Picking 'warm' misses that the harm is from the light, not from heat.

applications: Swab tests in hospitals and food factories use firefly luciferase to measure ATP, and so tell if living germs are left on a surface.
Scientists attach green fluorescent protein to other proteins to watch nerve cells grow and cancer cells spread.
Glowing bacteria are used to test water, because a poison in the water makes them dim.
Doctors use enzymes in medicine and in blood tests, and keep them cool because heat would bend them out of shape.
Astronomers and sailors use a dim red lamp at night so that their eyes stay used to the dark.
Shopkeepers and banks use UV torches to check notes and documents for parts that glow under UV.
Washing powder makers add chemicals that send out blue-white light under UV, so clothes look whiter.
Engineers study how a firefly's lantern lets out so much light, to make better LED lamps.
Beach towns and turtle groups use low, shaded amber lamps to protect hatchling turtles.
Scientists who study the sea use red lights and camera traps so that deep-sea animals do not see them and swim away.
Cities that join the dark sky movement use shielded lamps that point down, so people see the stars again.
Computer scientists copy the way fireflies line up to make groups of sensors keep time together with no master clock.

open_questions.q: How exactly do fireflies in a tree line up their flashes?
open_questions.why_open: Computer models show that a simple rule can do it. Scientists are still working out which rule each kind of firefly really follows.

open_questions.q: Where does a firefly get their luciferin from, and how do they make it?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that fireflies have luciferin, but the full set of steps by which they make it inside their bodies is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: Why did fireflies and other beings first begin to glow?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody was there to watch. Scientists have ideas, such as a warning or a way to deal with oxygen, but they cannot yet test them.

open_questions.q: What causes the huge winter blooms of sea sparkle in the Arabian Sea, and what do they do to the fish?
open_questions.why_open: Warm water, nutrients and low-oxygen water may all play a part. Many more years of careful records are needed.

open_questions.q: How many deep-sea animals use light we cannot see, such as red light or ultraviolet?
open_questions.why_open: Most of the deep sea has never been visited, and the cameras we use are made for light that our eyes can see.

open_questions.q: Do other animals also use something like quorum sensing to count their crowd?
open_questions.why_open: Bacteria are known to count their crowd this way. Scientists are still looking for the same idea in other living things.

open_questions.q: What is it like to be a firefly, or a crowd of fireflies flashing as one?
open_questions.why_open: Science can measure what fireflies do. What it is like to be one is a question that no instrument can answer yet.
