maths.problem: In a made-up Eyes in the Dark test, a child saw the glow through 3 sheets at 1 minute, 5 at 5 minutes, 7 at 10 minutes and 9 at 20 minutes. How many more sheets could the child see through at 20 minutes than at 1 minute? How many times as many is that?
maths.answer: 6 more sheets, and 3 times as many.
maths.explain: 9 sheets at 20 minutes take away 3 sheets at 1 minute is 6. The child saw through 9 sheets after 20 minutes and 3 sheets after 1 minute. 9 divided by 3 is 3. So the child saw through 3 times as many sheets.
maths.context: In the Eyes in the Dark test, you hide a glow stick under sheets of paper and count how many sheets you can see the glow through at different times.

chart.title: Made-up example: sheets the glow could be seen through

maths.why_maths: Taking one number away from another and dividing them shows how big the change in your eyes was, in two different ways.

maths.problem: An old bulb turns about 5 of every 100 parts of its energy into light. In a lab test, about 40 of every 100 firefly luciferin molecules that reacted gave out a flash. About how many times better is the firefly at that one step?
maths.explain: The bulb gives 5 parts in 100. The reaction gives 40 parts in 100. 40 divided by 5 is 8. So at that step, the firefly's reaction is about 8 times as good at making light as the old bulb. But the firefly still spends food energy, so the whole animal is not 8 times as efficient.
maths.context: This is about cold light. An old bulb wastes most of its energy as heat. A firefly's reaction wastes much less at the moment of light.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two parts out of 100 is the fair way to compare lights that use different amounts of energy.

maths.problem: In a made-up potato test, the raw cubes made a foam 4 centimetres high, and the cold raw cubes made a foam 2 centimetres high. What fraction of the raw foam was the cold foam? What does it show about cold?
maths.answer: One half. Cold slowed the enzyme but did not stop it.
maths.explain: The cold foam was 2 centimetres and the raw foam was 4 centimetres. 2 out of 4 is the same as 1 out of 2, which is one half. The cold potato still made foam, so cold only slowed the enzyme down. Boiling made no foam at all, because boiling bends the enzyme.
maths.context: In the Helper That Heat Stops test, you compare how much foam raw, boiled and cold potato cubes make in peroxide.
maths.why_maths: Writing one result as a fraction of another shows how much a change slowed the enzyme, without needing the exact units.

maths.problem: In the Crowd and the Signal activity, a glass of 200 millilitres needed 2 spoonfuls of signal water to look coloured. A jug holds 2 litres, which is 10 times as much water. About how many spoonfuls would the jug need?
maths.explain: 2 litres is 2,000 millilitres, and 2,000 divided by 200 is 10. The jug holds 10 times as much water. So it needs about 10 times as much signal. 2 spoonfuls times 10 is 20 spoonfuls.
maths.context: In the Crowd and the Signal activity, spoonfuls of coloured water stand for the signal that glowing bacteria give out. A glass stands for a tiny squid light organ and a jug for the open sea.
maths.why_maths: If the space is 10 times bigger, the signal you need is 10 times bigger. Multiplying shows why a crowd in a tiny space can count itself, and one in the open sea cannot.

maths.problem: One firefly flashes every 6 ticks and another every 8 ticks, and both start at tick 0 in the Flash Together game with the ignore rule. At which tick do they next flash at the same time?
maths.explain: The first firefly flashes at 6, 12, 18, 24 and so on. The second flashes at 8, 16, 24 and so on. The first number in both lists is 24. So they flash together next at tick 24, and then not again until tick 48.
maths.context: In the Flash Together game, fireflies with different beats only flash together by chance when nobody joins another's flash.
maths.why_maths: Finding the first multiple that two numbers share shows how rarely two different beats match by luck, and why a joining rule is needed.

maths.problem: Each of your eyes has about 100 million rod cells and about 5 million cone cells. About how many times as many rod cells as cone cells is that?
maths.explain: 100 million divided by 5 million is 20. You can check it. 5 million times 20 is 100 million. So there are about 20 rod cells for every cone cell, which is why you can see in dim light better than you can see colours.
maths.context: This is about the two kinds of light catchers in the retina. Rod cells work in dim light and cone cells work in bright light and see colour.
maths.why_maths: Dividing big numbers shows how many more rod cells than cone cells there are, which helps explain why night sight is good and night colour is poor.

maths.problem: In a made-up star count, a family counted 2 stars with the lights on, 6 stars after switching off the lights and waiting 20 minutes, and 24 stars from a dark village. How many times as many stars did they see in the village as after waiting at home?
maths.explain: 24 divided by 6 is 4. You can check it by counting in sixes: 6, 12, 18, 24. That is four sixes. So the dark village showed 4 times as many stars as the home after waiting, and 12 times as many as with the lights on.
maths.context: In the How Dark Is Our Sky project, you count the stars in a card window on three nights with different amounts of light.

chart.title: Made-up example: stars counted in the card window

maths.why_maths: Dividing one count by another shows how much of the sky was lost to lights, in a way that works for any card size.

maths.problem: A bobtail squid pushes out 9 tenths of her 1,000 glowing bacteria at dawn. The bacteria that are left double every hour. After 3 hours, how many bacteria are there?
maths.explain: 9 tenths of 1,000 is 900, so 1,000 take away 900 leaves 100. After 1 hour there are 200, after 2 hours 400, and after 3 hours 800. These are made-up numbers, but real squid also refill their light organ each day.
maths.context: This is about the squid and her glowing bacteria. Each dawn the squid pushes out most of the bacteria, and the few left multiply again during the day.
maths.why_maths: Taking a fraction and then doubling shows how fast a small group can grow back, which is how the squid's lamp refills.

maths.problem: Red light is nearly gone within about 10 metres of sea water. A diver goes down to 35 metres. How many metres below the depth where red is gone is the diver? What colour of light is left?
maths.answer: 25 metres below. Mostly blue and some green are left.
maths.explain: 35 take away 10 is 25. So the diver is 25 metres below the place where red light has gone. Green and blue travel further than red, and so at that depth mostly blue and a little green are left.
maths.context: This is about the colours of light in the sea. Water takes in red light first, and blue light goes the deepest.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting depths tells you how far below the red light you are, so you can tell which colours are left.

roots.context: We have followed living light from a firefly's chemistry to the eye that reads it, and to a crowd of fireflies flashing as one. Now we ask what that tells us about leaders, crowds and ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: Thousands of fireflies can flash as one with no leader. In the Flash Together game, each player followed one rule: join a flash you see, if your marker is at halfway or further. The group lined up fast with that rule, and never lined up without it. So a crowd acts as one through how its members answer each other, not through any one member.
deep_truth.habit: We think that when many things act together, one of them must be in charge, or must have given the signal.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Flash Together game, players with different beats flashed together within about 20 ticks, when each one joined the flashes they saw. In the round where they ignored each other, they never lined up in 40 ticks. If your own rounds went differently, write them down as they are and play again.

three.who_am_i: The cells that keep your heart beating are a crowd with no boss. Each pacemaker cell answers its neighbours, and together they keep one beat.
three.what_is_life: One glowing bacterium cannot make a visible light. A crowd, counting itself with a signal chemical, can light a squid's lamp.
three.what_is_this_world: In 1665, Christiaan Huygens saw two pendulum clocks on one wall swing in step. The wall carried a tiny push between them, and that was enough.

roots.thread: A firefly's flash is chemistry that turns into light. Your eye turns that light back into chemistry. A crowd of fireflies lines up because each one sees the others. A squid and her bacteria share one lamp because each does a part the other cannot. In all these cases, what happens is not inside any one being. It happens between them, in the light they send to each other and in the way they answer. Science can follow each step. The question that remains is what a crowd is, if it has no leader and no centre.

science.text: A firefly's flash needs luciferin, luciferase, oxygen and ATP. Light starts when the molecules react, and your rod cells turn that light back into a chemical signal.
Some fireflies flash in step because each has a timer and adjusts it when they see a neighbour flash. Models show that this one rule is enough, but the details are not known for every kind.
What it is like to be a firefly, or a crowd of fireflies, is not something science can measure yet.

other_view.view: A flashing tree is just many separate fireflies, each with a timer and a simple rule. The crowd is not a thing. Calling it one is only a way of speaking, and nothing more needs to be said. That is an honest and careful view.

how_we_found_out.story: In the 1880s, Raphael Dubois showed that a glow needs two chemicals, a fuel and a helper. After that, many scientists thought that luciferin, luciferase and oxygen were all that a firefly needed. But in a test tube the glow was weak, and it died away fast. In 1947, the American scientist William McElroy worked with extract from firefly lanterns. He saw that the glow faded when the extract stood for a while. Then he tried adding small molecules from living cells, one at a time. Only one brought the glow back: ATP, the energy carrier of all cells. So the old idea was incomplete. A flash needs a payment of cell energy as well. Today firefly luciferase is used in hospitals and laboratories to measure ATP, and so to tell whether living cells are present.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many scientists thought luciferin, luciferase and oxygen were enough to make a firefly's glow. McElroy showed that without ATP the glow fades, and that adding ATP brings it back.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home by a family. Flash Together was checked with a computer model of the same rules: with 2 to 4 players and start numbers 0 to 6, the listen rule lined the group up in 9 to 19 ticks every time, and the ignore rule never did in 40 ticks. Real players will be slower and may slip in counting, which is fine. Eyes in the Dark needs a room that is really dark. A bathroom with no window and a towel at the door works. The numbers of sheets are a guess from the physics of light and paper, so the example is made up, and the parent note says what to do if all 12 sheets are seen through. The potato test needs a fresh bottle of 3 percent peroxide. Many Indian chemist bottles say 6 percent or 20 volume, and the steps say to dilute them. If the raw potato does not fizz, the bottle is old. A grown-up does the boiling and the peroxide. Glow Detective needs a UV torch, so it is outside the core path. Look Beside It may show only a one or two sheet difference, and the note says to write down no difference if there is none. Facts to verify before release: the 2008 firefly quantum yield of about 41 percent, the 1947 McElroy ATP finding, Eisner's 1997 report on Photuris, the Gonyaulax rhythm work of Hastings and Sweeney, the Gomes 2014 Arabian Sea paper, the claim that red light is nearly gone within about 10 metres, the figures of about 100 million rod cells and 5 million cone cells, and the statement that Olive Ridley volunteer groups work on the Chennai coast.
